item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
CESENATICO / MALI LOŠINJ - Every year in the northern Adriatic, hundreds of loggerhead turtles and dozens of bottlenose dolphins die in Italian and Croatian fishing nets. They are protected species under EU law, and only 250–400 dolphins live in these waters. Officially it is "accidental" bycatch. In practice it happens every day, on both coasts, and almost nobody reports it.

This cross-border investigation shows how the shared sea between two EU member states has become a grey zone. Italian fishers blame Croatian fleets, and Croatian fishers blame the Italians. Monitoring is weak on both sides. Both countries face EU infringement procedures under the Habitats Directive; for Croatia, the formal notice came in February 2025.

The solutions exist and have already been paid for. For more than a decade the EU has funded trials of Turtle Excluder Devices, LED-lit gillnets and acoustic deterrents. NGOs and research centres from both coasts have worked with willing fishers to test them. Yet none of these measures has ever been made mandatory. Projects end, compensation for fishers stops, and the next grant starts again from scratch. Brussels pays for the solutions while opening infringement procedures for failing to apply them.

Key findings

Bycatch of protected turtles and dolphins in the northern Adriatic is routine and largely unreported, so official figures understate the real toll. Fishers on both coasts treat it as "part of the job" and have no incentive to declare it, while Italy and Croatia blame each other's fleets. Effective mitigation tools exist and have been tested with EU money for over a decade. None has been made mandatory, so protection depends on short-term projects that stop when the funding ends.

Methodology

The team reported on both coasts, from Riccione and Cesenatico in Italy to the Cres-Lošinj archipelago in Croatia. They worked with the Fondazione Cetacea and the Blue World Institute, which has monitored Adriatic dolphins since 1987. They interviewed fishers, researchers and rescue-centre staff, and examined EU-funded mitigation projects, EU infringement procedures and GFCM/ICES data on bycatch and overfishing. Because bycatch goes largely unreported, the official figures are a minimum, not the real toll.

Themes

  • Fishing industry

Publication

ONLINE

  • Il costo nascosto nella rete, da pesca, Startupbusiness, 21/10/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Croatia
  • Italy

Team members

Marta Abbà

Marta Abbà is an investigative journalists based in Milan.

Barbara Matejčić

Barbara Matejčić is a award-winning Croatian journalist, non-fiction writer and audio producer.

Elisabetta Zavoli

Elisabetta Zavoli is an Italian environmental documentary photographer.

Related projects

  • © Wikicommons

    European Fish Fraud in Namibia

    A Dutch fishing giant is involved in a corruption affair and tax evasion scheme concerning fishing quotas in Namibia. The money trail goes via Poland and Iceland.

    Meer lezen
  • © Regin Winther Poulsen and Agostino Petroni

    Pelagic Fishes Know No National Borders

    LONDON / BRUSSELS – According to a 1980 international UN law, the Northeastern Atlantic countries must meet regularly to agree on a fishing quota for each country––so that everybody gets a fair share and fish stocks don't get overfished. The multilateral agreements are supposed to ensure that no government exploits the moving fish resource within their borders.

    Meer lezen
  • © Bruna Casas

    The End of Mediterranean Artisanal Fishermen

    PALMA / ACI TREZZA / AGIA NAPA  – This investigation focuses on how the EU laws have promoted industrial fishing in the Mediterranean, to the detriment of Southern European small-scale fishermen.

    Meer lezen

Need resources for your own investigative story?

Journalismfund Europe's flexible grants programmes enable journalists to produce relevant public interest stories with a European mind-set from international, national, and regional perspectives.

Support independent cross-border investigative journalism

We rely on your support to continue the work that we do. Make a gift of any amount today.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
MILAN - [No] Zone di Sacrificio is an investigative and civic journalism project connecting Italian communities affected by industrial pollution, environmental damage and health inequalities. Through investigations, videos, podcasts, public data, scientific evidence and access-to-information tools, it brings local cases into the wider national and European debate on environmental justice, public health and the right to information.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

Project Activities

Alongside its institutional website, Cittadini Reattivi created a dedicated multimedia platform for [No] Zone di Sacrificio: click here

The platform brings together investigations, documents, videos, podcasts and subsequent updates, keeping the stories accessible and connected over time.

The project developed a series of multimedia investigations across different Italian territories, combining field reporting, interviews, environmental and health data, scientific studies, FOIA requests, administrative documents and court decisions.

The investigations did not simply catalogue polluted areas. Each case was reconstructed through its specific history, industrial legacy, environmental and health impacts, legal developments, civic mobilisation and possible paths towards change.

In Torviscosa, “Torviscosa, l’eredità della città-fabbrica” reconstructed the legacy of the industrial company town built around the SNIA-Caffaro production system, following the history of contamination, remediation and the relationship between the industrial site, its waterways and the Marano lagoon: click here

In Brescia, “La primavera di Brescia” examined another major legacy of the Caffaro chemical industry, focusing on contamination, remediation, health, memory and the long civic and institutional process that has developed around one of Italy’s best-known contaminated Sites of National Interest: click here

In Valle del Sacco, the reporting followed both the still unresolved contamination of the Site of National Interest and the work of communities trying to build alternatives through environmental protection, health prevention, culture and territorial reconversion: click here

Click here!

In Casale Monferrato, the project examined the legacy of Eternit asbestos from two complementary perspectives: the city as a laboratory of democracy, where civic mobilisation, institutions and public-health policies have generated concrete responses, and the continuing judicial struggle showing why justice for asbestos victims is still unfinished:

  • Click here!
  • Click here!

In Bologna, “Amianto, la strage infinita dell’ex OGR di Bologna” reconstructed the history of the former Officine Grandi Riparazioni railway workshops, the consequences of asbestos exposure among workers and the continuing struggle for recognition, memory and justice: click here

The project also investigated the legacy of the former OGR in another territorial context through “Quel che resta dell’ex OGR”: click here

In Terra dei Fuochi, the project combined the historical reconstruction of one of Italy’s most significant environmental crises with reporting on communities that have moved from denunciation to civic monitoring, legal action and the construction of local responses. The case was also followed in light of the European Court of Human Rights judgment condemning Italy for failing to adequately protect citizens from environmental risks:

Click here!

Click here!

In Salerno, the project documented decades of conflict around the Fonderie Pisano in the Valle dell’Irno, including pollution concerns, health impacts, court decisions and a long civic mobilisation: click here

The project subsequently followed the mobilisation that led to the closure of the plant: click here

Reporting on the case has continued beyond the funded period, following the closure, judicial developments, remediation and the debate over the future use of the area.

In Falconara Marittima, “Falconara, dove le bonifiche non arrivano al mare” focused on a territory where industrial contamination and remediation reach the Adriatic coast, following the refinery, the environmental legacy of the industrial site and the new phase opened by its acquisition by SOCAR, the state-owned oil company of Azerbaijan: click here

In the Susa Valley, “Valsusa, la grande opera che non passa” examined the decades-long conflict surrounding the Turin–Lyon railway infrastructure, looking not only at the project itself but also at environmental impacts, public spending, territorial opposition and the democratic implications of a major public work that continues to divide the valley: click here

Although these investigations are rooted in specific local territories, many – if not all – of the issues they address have a direct European dimension. These are local stories, but their causes, consequences and possible solutions are closely connected to European environmental and public-health policies, industrial regulation, access to information, workers’ rights, the use of public funds and the enforcement of EU and human-rights law.

From the European Court of Human Rights judgments concerning environmental protection in Campania to EU rules on industrial emissions and remediation, from major infrastructure policies to the role of multinational and state-owned companies, the cases investigated by [No] Zone di Sacrificio show how decisions taken at European level have concrete consequences in local communities – and how conflicts originating in apparently peripheral territories can raise questions that concern Europe as a whole.

This local-to-European perspective became one of the central elements of the project: connecting what happens in a neighbourhood, a factory, a contaminated site or a valley with the wider European debate on environmental justice, democracy, public health and the right of citizens to know and participate in decisions affecting their lives.

Taranto became the clearest and most extensive example of this European dimension. “Taranto, la zona di sacrificio che l’Europa non può più ignorare” followed the former ILVA steelworks through its environmental and health impacts, workers’ conditions, public expenditure, remediation, institutional decisions and the long sequence of Italian and European legal proceedings: click here

The investigative work developed through [No] Zone di Sacrificio has continued beyond the funded period. The Taranto case became the basis for Rosy Battaglia’s long-form investigation “Qual è la vera posta in gioco a Taranto”, published by the independent Italian media outlet Valigia Blu on 29 August 2026. The article brings together more than a decade of reporting and reconstructs a case involving the European Court of Human Rights, the Court of Justice of the European Union, the European Commission infringement procedure and the latest Italian judicial developments: click here

[No] Zone di Sacrificio is therefore already continuing as a living editorial project. New developments are being followed and published, as shown by recent updates from Taranto and Salerno.

The project also developed a multimedia and participatory dimension through video interviews with experts, podcasts and webinars addressing the legal, scientific, health and social dimensions of living in contaminated territories.

The complete podcast archive is available here: click here

The project video playlist is available here: click here

Among the expert interviews:

  • “Zone di sacrificio, bonifiche e diritto al futuro”, with Giuseppe Vadalà: click here
  • “Zone di sacrificio e salute pubblica”, with Fabrizio Bianchi: click here
  • “Zone di sacrificio: quali strade abbiamo davvero per uscire dalla crisi ambientale?”, with Walter Ganapini: click here
  • “Vittimizzazione ambientale”, with Rosalba Altopiedi: click here
  • “Ambiente, salute e potere”, with Vittorio Martone: click here

The project also organised webinars designed as tools for civic information and participation:

  • “Vivere in un SIN inquinato: cosa può fare la legge per te”, with lawyer Massimo Moretti: click here
  • “Come esercitare la cittadinanza scientifica nel nostro tempo”, with Prof. Daniela Vellutino: click here
  • “Ambiente e salute nei SIN: dalla comunicazione alla partecipazione”, with Liliana Cori: click here
  • Community contributions and co-produced reporting were also published through “Voci dalle Comunità”: click here

At the same time, Cittadini Reattivi is planning a new phase of in-person dissemination, bringing the investigations, videos, podcasts and documentary materials into schools and back to the communities involved, as well as to universities, festivals and public meetings. The aim is to extend the circulation and educational value of the journalism produced through PM4D and use it as a tool for environmental information, civic participation and scientific citizenship.

What is the impact?

[No] Zone di Sacrificio addressed a particular form of news desert: territories that are not necessarily without media coverage, but where complex environmental and public-health issues often lack continuous, independent and specialised journalism.

Many of the communities investigated have lived for decades alongside industrial contamination, asbestos, polluted land, remediation delays or major infrastructure conflicts. These places often return to national attention only after an accident, a court ruling or a political controversy. What tends to disappear between these moments is the long history of exposure, scientific evidence, public decisions, judicial proceedings and the experiences of the people who live there.

The project sought to fill this gap by connecting local knowledge with public documents, scientific research, data and investigative reporting, and by following cases over time rather than treating them as isolated news events.

There is also another dimension to this information gap. Issues arising in peripheral or highly localised territories are often perceived and reported as exclusively local problems, even when they are closely linked to European legislation, institutions, policies and public resources.

[No] Zone di Sacrificio sought to make these connections visible. The industrial legacy of Caffaro in Brescia and Torviscosa, the long civic mobilisation around Fonderie Pisano in Salerno, the environmental and institutional conflicts in Falconara, Terra dei Fuochi, Casale Monferrato, Valle del Sacco, the Susa Valley and Taranto became parts of a shared national and European narrative.

In this sense, countering news deserts also meant preventing these territories from becoming isolated information islands. The project connected local evidence and community knowledge with broader questions of European environmental justice, public health, industrial regulation, access to information, public expenditure and democratic participation.

Taranto demonstrates this particularly clearly: what can appear as a local industrial dispute is in fact a European case involving environmental law, public health, workers, public expenditure and decisions by European courts and institutions. The Valigia Blu investigation published on 29 August extends that work beyond the project platform and brings the case to a broader national audience.

The project created a shared editorial space for communities whose experiences and knowledge are often fragmented across local news, scientific studies, administrative documents and court proceedings.

Citizens, researchers, doctors, activists and local organisations were not treated simply as sources for individual stories. They became part of an ongoing network that enables Cittadini Reattivi to receive new documentation, follow legal and institutional developments and connect experiences from different Italian territories.

One of the project’s contributions was also to show communities that what happens in their territory is not necessarily an isolated local issue. By connecting individual cases with national and European policies, legislation, institutions and similar experiences elsewhere, the project helped place local knowledge within a wider public-interest framework.

The multimedia approach made complex information available in different formats through investigations, videos, podcasts, expert interviews, webinars and community-generated contributions. This helped make environmental, health and legal issues accessible beyond specialist audiences.

The end of the PM4D grant did not mark the end of the editorial project. [No] Zone di Sacrificio is already being updated as new developments emerge in the territories, as shown by the recent reporting on Taranto and Salerno.

Cittadini Reattivi is also planning in-person activities to bring the investigations and multimedia material back to schools and the communities involved, as well as to universities, festivals and public meetings. This next phase is intended to give the journalism produced through PM4D a longer public life: not only keeping investigations accessible online, but returning the knowledge gathered through the reporting process to the people and territories that helped produce it.

The PM4D support was particularly important in the current Italian media environment, where resources and spaces available for long-term independent investigative journalism are increasingly limited. For a small non-profit media organisation such as Cittadini Reattivi, the grant was fundamental in making it possible to dedicate professional time and editorial resources to complex investigations that require continuity, specialised knowledge and sustained engagement with communities.

Project Links

  • [No] Zone di Sacrificio – dedicated project platform
  • Stories archive
  • Project page and grant credits
  • Podcast archive
  • YouTube project playlist
  • Voices from the Communities
  • Cittadini Reattivi
  • LiberaeCivica newsletter
  • Valigia Blu – “Qual è la vera posta in gioco a Taranto”

Project Pictures

Photos by Rosy Battaglia

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
VRANJE - With the support of the project, Slobodna reč strengthened public-interest journalism in southern Serbia by bringing overlooked local issues to the attention of citizens and decision-makers. Reporting focused on child safety, cultural heritage, social inequality, and vulnerable communities, including those in underserved municipalities such as Surdulica and Preševo.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

Project-related content generated close to one million views across platforms, while short-form video significantly expanded the outlet's reach among younger audiences. Several stories prompted institutional responses, wider media coverage, and civic engagement, demonstrating the impact of independent local journalism in communities often overlooked by larger media.

Project Activities

Slobodna reč produced field-based public-interest stories on child safety, cultural heritage, gender inequality, vulnerable groups, abandoned animals and neglected infrastructure. Reporting combined field visits, interviews, document analysis and follow-up on institutional responses.

The project also produced 12 short-form videos and expanded distribution from Facebook and Instagram to TikTok and YouTube Shorts. Training young interns and hands-on work strengthened the team's filming and editing skills. Social media promotion and cooperation with other media significantly increased the visibility of the stories and helped reach communities and audiences beyond Vranje.

What is the impact?

The project helped address the effects of the news desert in southern Serbia by providing consistent public-interest reporting from a region that receives limited attention from national media. Slobodna reč covered communities and issues that are frequently overlooked, including other multicultural municipalities in district and rural areas. Several stories were republished by other media, and some received national coverage, extending local issues beyond their place of origin. Digital distribution and short-form video also helped connect local journalism with younger audiences and reduce geographical barriers to access.

The project increased the visibility of local problems and contributed to concrete responses. Reporting on a dangerous area near a school was followed by the installation of protective fencing after more than a decade without action. Coverage of traffic safety near a rural school prompted commitments from authorities, while reporting on a historic school property generated public debate and civic engagement. Audience growth was also significant: Facebook followers increased by 31% and Instagram followers by 45%, while project content generated close to one million views. The launch of TikTok and YouTube Shorts further expanded reach among younger audiences.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BUENOS AIRES / BERLIN / ROME / PARIS - Vaca Muerta is a vast area of Argentine Patagonia, home to the world’s second-largest reserve of unconventional natural gas and the fourth-largest reserve of unconventional oil. In 2012, the Argentine government began investing in the region, with the stated aim of using these resources primarily to meet the country’s domestic energy needs.

Over the years, however, the situation has changed. Today, foreign companies, particularly European energy corporations, play a significant role in the exploitation of Vaca Muerta’s oil and gas reserves. There are currently more than 2,600 active wells in the area. While these operations are presented as an opportunity for economic growth and energy development, they have also caused serious social and environmental harm, including land and water pollution, health problems among local residents, and the displacement of Indigenous communities from their ancestral territories.

Since 2012, under the Peronist government led by Cristina Kirchner, gas and oil have been extracted in the area using fracking, a technique that allows fossil fuels trapped in layers of rock to be extracted by injecting water, sand and chemicals at high pressure, fracturing the rock and releasing the hydrocarbons. Fracking is a particularly invasive technique for the environment and, according to numerous scientific studies, can cause serious environmental and health problems for people living near oil wells, including respiratory and skin problems, cancer, congenital abnormalities, miscarriages and pregnancy complications.

For years, residents, Indigenous communities and scientists have been raising concerns and protesting against the consequences of extraction, with their demands largely ignored by both the Argentine government and the companies operating in the region. This investigation examines the role of foreign, particularly European, energy companies in Vaca Muerta and the human and environmental costs of their operations.

Key findings

  • Map of European companies operating in the area.
  • Map of European countries importing gas and oil from the area.
  • Percentage of gas and oil exported to European countries.
  • Cases of people suffering from illnesses that may be caused by fracking.
  • Residents whose homes have been damaged by repeated earth tremors that may be caused by fracking.
  • Indigenous communities fighting against companies that have drilled wells on their ancestral lands.

Methodology

The first part of this investigation focused on mapping the foreign companies operating in Vaca Muerta: who they are, who owns their capital, which countries it comes from, which European countries they export to, in what proportions, and since what year they have been operating in the area.

We then went on to identify the human rights and environmental issues affecting the region. To document these, we conducted over 40 interviews with victims, scientists, political authorities, NGOs and communities of the Indigenous peoples of the area.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • The hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sickness, The Guardian, 15/10/2026

More to come

AUDIO

  • Seidisera, Rsi, 15/07/2026

COUNTRIES

  • Argentina
  • France
  • Germany
  • Italy

Team members

Elena Basso

Elena Basso is an Italian freelance journalist based in Chile.

Erica Canepa

Erica Canepa is an Italian documentary photographer based in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Micaela Ryan

Micaela Ryan is a filmmaker, audiovisual producer, and photographer.

Related projects

  • © Michael Buchsbaum

    How Carbon Capture Is a Gift To Big Oil

    LONDON – With Europe reeling from heat waves and wildfires, the EU is backing projects to capture industrial emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) as a key pillar in its fight against climate change. But what if these multi-billion-euro schemes make the problem worse?

    Meer lezen
  • © Daniela Sala

    Oil and Gas Majors Fuelling Ecocide Worldwide

    PARIS - 7,000 protected areas are under threat from oil and gas projects worldwide. 120 countries were included in the investigation data analysed by a large cross-border team of independent journalists and media outlets.

    Meer lezen
  • © Emily Garthwaite

    Toxic Skies, Dirty Waters

    QAYYARAH – Wedged between an oil field and a refinery, this Iraqi town has paid the price for its country's petroleum wealth for decades. The facilities blanket the surrounding air with toxic gases and pump oily wastewater into the adjacent Tigris River. The industry that gave Qayyarah its existence is now threatening the health of everyone who lives there.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
VIGO / TAIWAN – Spain and Taiwan together account for close to two thirds of the world’s reported blue shark catch, turning one of the ocean’s most widely distributed predators into a global commodity.

This investigation follows the blue shark from longline fleets in the Atlantic and Pacific to the processing halls of Galicia and the shark-fin trade in Taiwan. It traces a supply chain in which almost every part of the animal has a market: the meat is sold across Europe and beyond, while the fins enter an Asian trade that persists despite falling demand in some of its traditional markets.

At the heart of the investigation is the industry’s claim that blue shark fishing is sustainable. In much of the world, the species is still caught without any overall catch limit. In the North Atlantic, where quotas do exist, the latest assessment puts the probability that the stock is already overfished at 50.1 per cent – essentially a coin toss. The investigation shows how scientific uncertainty, weak data and political negotiation allow millions of blue sharks to remain part of a lucrative global trade.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Teure Flossen, billiges Fleisch, Süddeutsche Zeitung, 16/10/2026

More to come

    NOUAKCHOTT - In the imbalance of power in Europe’s fishing deals with West African countries, locals get the short end of the stick.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
KECSKEMET - Through the PM4D-supported project, KecsUP strengthened its public-interest reporting on marginalised communities and underrepresented social issues in Kecskemét and the wider region. The project expanded the "Living on the Fringe" / "Peremhelyzetek" section and launched KecsUP Next, a newsroom-based programme for young contributors. Four young people became more deeply involved in editorial work, and the newsroom produced 18 thematic articles on social vulnerability, exclusion and local public-interest issues.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

The section also published articles by the young contributors themselves, including stories on topics directly relevant to their own generation. The project helped KecsUP reach communities that are often missing from local public debate and created a tested model for involving young people in independent local journalism.

Project Activities

With the support of the grant, KecsUP implemented four closely connected activities.

First, it strengthened its "Living on the Fringe" / "Peremhelyzetek" section, which focuses on marginalised groups, social vulnerability and local public-interest issues also affecting young people. During the project period, 18 thematic articles were published within this framework, covering topics such as disability and accessibility, autism, Roma integration, LGBTQ communities, homelessness, alcohol addiction, social support and the labour market situation of young people starting their careers.

Second, KecsUP launched the KecsUP Next / Young Reporters Welcome! internship programme. Its aim was to recruit, select, train and mentor young participants. The selection process consisted of several stages, including DISC profiling, personal interviews and practical assignments. Instead of the originally planned two young participants, four interns became more deeply involved in the programme.

Third, the young contributors received practical training and continuous editorial mentoring. They took part in training sessions on journalism, photography, video and podcast production, online journalism and social media. Through the mentoring process, they were gradually integrated into real newsroom workflows: they prepared press reviews, worked on interviews, produced vox pop-style reports, participated in KecsUP events and wrote their own articles. As part of the programme, they also joined KecsUP's election results event, attended live public events and visited the newsroom of 24.hu.

Fourth, the project strengthened youth audience engagement and community-oriented editorial participation. The young contributors produced content on social issues affecting their own generation and local communities. This process was supported by a dedicated KecsUP Next subpage, online questionnaires, offline posters placed at high-traffic locations in Kecskemét and social media communication. In addition to the articles counted towards the project, the interns also contributed to several other editorial materials, showing that the impact of the project went beyond the minimum planned deliverables and helped young contributors become integrated into the everyday work of the newsroom.

What is the impact?

The impact of the project can primarily be evaluated through the way it strengthened KecsUP’s role in a region where the phenomenon of news deserts remains a real concern. In Kecskemét and the wider region, it is particularly important to have an independent local newsroom that does not only report on day-to-day political events, but also consistently covers social issues, vulnerable groups and stories that are often pushed to the margins of local public debate.

With the support of PM4D, KecsUP strengthened its “Living on the Fringe” / “Peremhelyzetek” section as a public-interest journalism product. During the project, topics such as disability and accessibility, autism, Roma integration, LGBTQ communities, homelessness, alcohol addiction, social support and the labour market difficulties of young people starting their careers became part of the local public conversation. Covering issues affecting the younger generation was an especially important part of this effort, as the project aimed not only to reach young readers, but also to bring young people’s own experiences and questions into the local public sphere. The project did not solve the problem of news deserts on its own, but it made a concrete contribution by ensuring that more sensitive, socially relevant and locally grounded public-interest content became available in the region.

One of the most important positive changes brought by the project was that young people appeared in KecsUP’s work not only as a target audience, but also as active authors, interviewers and community actors. The KecsUP Next programme gave young contributors the opportunity to learn in real newsroom situations, bring in their own topics, conduct interviews, participate in events and report on issues that also affect their own generation. This supported not only the professional development of the participants, but also helped bring young people’s experiences and questions closer to the local public sphere.

For the wider community, the project created positive change by making people, groups and life situations that are often pushed to the margins of local public debate more consistently visible. The articles published in the “Living on the Fringe” / “Peremhelyzetek” section addressed social vulnerability, acceptance, accessibility, minority situations, social problems and difficulties affecting young people. In this way, the project contributed to a more sensitive, nuanced and human-centred local public conversation in Kecskemét and the wider region.

  • Instagram
  • YouTube

  • Hungary

Media

KecsUP News

KecsUP News is a grassroots non-profit organisation founded in 2019 in Kecskemét. 

Related projects

  • Lisboa Without Borders: A Newsletter for Lisbon’s Immigrants

    LISBOA -  Mensagem de Lisboa launched and developed three editions of Lisboa Without Borders, an English-language newsletter focused on Lisbon’s foreign communities. The project took feedback from community members into consideration to deliver content that migrants in Lisbon previously lacked.

    Meer lezen
  • © Re:Baltica

    Regional Voices: Reliable News Before Municipal Elections

    RIGA - The project strengthened access to independent local journalism in three municipalities underserved by independent media — Riga, Daugavpils, and Rēzekne — during the pre-municipal election period. It reached young people, women, and Russian-speaking audiences with reliable political and investigative reporting ahead of the municipal elections. The project also strengthened direct connections between journalists and local communities, particularly in Daugavpils and Rēzekne.

    Meer lezen
  • © Szegeder

    Empowering Local Voices: Strengthening Szegeder’s Engagement and Sustainability

    SZEGED - With PM4D support, Szegeder developed new tools for reader participation and personalised newsletters, while launching a new high-quality interview format focused on people shaping life in Szeged. The project strengthened both its digital infrastructure and its ability to produce distinctive, community-focused local journalism.

    Meer lezen

In this way, the project contributed to a more sensitive, nuanced and human-centred local public conversation in Kecskemét and the wider region.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
MIELEC – AWR Korso turned a largely absent local topic into a sustained public conversation about Roma history, culture and contemporary life in Mielec. The project produced 60 articles and 11 podcast episodes, supported by research, workshops and educational resources, while giving Roma participants space to tell their own stories. It reached new audiences and built lasting relationships between the Roma community, local institutions, educators, researchers and the media. All outputs remain freely accessible through a dedicated online knowledge hub.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

Project Activities

AWR Korso began the project with three diagnostic surveys and one evaluation survey, which gathered 254 responses, as well as 19 in-depth interviews. The findings helped the editorial team identify information gaps, understand attitudes towards the Roma community and develop a publication plan responding to the audience’s actual needs.

The project resulted in 60 articles, exceeding the planned target of 50, and 11 published podcast episodes instead of the eight initially planned. Three additional episodes were prepared for publication after the end of the grant period. Six online training recordings, four podcasts created during workshops and six audio summaries were also produced.

Roma representatives, children, young people, educators, seniors, social organisations, cultural institutions, local government representatives, researchers and regional media took part in the activities. Cooperation with the Radosna Żyrafa integration day-room was particularly important, as it created a shared space for Roma and non-Roma children and adults.

A multi-channel campaign promoted the project through regional news websites, social media, Radio Leliwa, local newspapers, newsletters and outdoor activities. Promotional materials generated more than 255,000 views, while the campaign on the Korso.pl Facebook profile alone reached more than 111,000 unique users.

The project also strengthened AWR Korso’s capacity to produce public-interest journalism. A podcast studio, financed from the organisation’s own resources, was created and will continue to support social, educational and civic media projects. All journalistic, research and educational materials were collected on a dedicated website, ensuring free and long-term access to the project’s results.

What is the impact?

Before the project began, the Roma community was only sporadically represented in the local media, usually in connection with isolated events, conflicts or stereotypes. There was no systematic source of information about Roma history, culture, identity, education and contemporary life, nor a space where Roma representatives could present their experiences in their own voices.

The project filled this local information gap by creating a substantial body of reliable public-interest journalism based on research, interviews and direct cooperation with the Roma community. Its 60 articles, podcasts, research findings and educational materials form a permanent, freely accessible knowledge base for residents, teachers, researchers, social organisations and other media. The project therefore reduced a topic-specific news desert while making the local media landscape more inclusive and pluralistic.

The most important change was the development of trust between the editorial team and members of the Roma community. At the beginning, some participants approached media cooperation cautiously and were reluctant to appear publicly. Over time, their willingness to participate in interviews, podcasts, research and educational activities increased. Roma participants were able to tell their own stories instead of being described solely from an institutional or external perspective.

The project also brought together the Roma community, educators, social organisations, local government, cultural institutions, researchers and residents. These relationships have continued beyond the funding period. The project led to cooperation with academic institutions, an invitation to share its results in the journal “Studia Romologica”, and participation in scientific and cultural events devoted to Roma history and culture.

For the wider audience, the project provided access to reliable knowledge about a community that had previously received little sustained media coverage. It encouraged a more informed and substantive discussion of Roma issues and demonstrated interest in longer journalistic formats, including podcasts. While lasting social change requires more time than a single grant cycle, the project created a strong foundation for continued dialogue, cooperation and intercultural education.

  • Poznajmy się - wszyscy jesteśmy braćmi i żyjemy pod wspólnym niebem
  • Wnioski po wywiadach pogłębionych (IDI)

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
GELDERSE VALLEI – Over several months, the team spent time with residents of a run-down high-rise development in the Dutch city of Ede. By engaging with residents, they discovered stories of resilience and community power, including a group of women who had built a self-support network that had been largely overlooked by aid workers.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

Projelct Activities

Through a collaboration with a local community worker, Bureau Spotlight was able to build close ties with a group of women in Ede-Zuid, a neighbourhood in the Dutch city of Ede. It developed methodologies for community-centred investigations that it can use for future investigations.

Bureau Spotlight published a series of six articles in a local newspaper and one feature story in a national newspaper, accompanied by documentary photography. All pieces were produced using a community-based approach.

For Bureau Spotlight, the project was a learning process. It tested whether community journalism can work within the context of investigative journalism, where time pressure often dominates. During the project, it encountered challenges around trust, access, and balancing openness with editorial independence. By reflecting on these experiences, it developed new ways of approaching sources, building networks, and working more relationally over a longer period of time. In this way, the project helped it move from a more 'extractive' approach toward a model based on sustained engagement. As a result, it is now better equipped to integrate community journalism methods into future investigative projects.

What is the impact?

The community Bureau Spotlight focused on is located in the Ede-Zuid neighbourhood, which is often described as a 'problem area' due to high crime rates and public disturbances. Media coverage and municipal reports tend to focus mainly on crime statistics and negative developments. But when Bureau Spotlight spoke with the people who live there, they said that they find it a pleasant place to live. They do not recognise themselves in the dominant narrative from local media and municipal reports.

By investing time in building relationships and listening to residents, Bureau Spotlight was able to include their perspectives in its reporting. In this way, it contributed to addressing a local "news desert" — not in the sense of a complete lack of coverage, but in the lack of nuanced, community-driven reporting. With its stories, Bureau Spotlight aims to add context and lived experience to the public debate about Ede-Zuid. It believes this broader and more balanced perspective is an essential part of serving its target audiences and strengthening local journalism.

Many of the women interviewed had never spoken to the media before, and for the first time their stories and perspectives on the neighbourhood were published in a local newspaper.

Bureau Spotlight believes it is important not only to give these women a voice, but also to ensure they feel heard and taken seriously. It hopes this experience helps them realise that their opinions and voices truly matter.

Many people in this community are not reached by local media; they have either disengaged over time or were never engaged in the first place. If they feel represented, they may be more inclined to follow and trust local media in the future. At the same time, Bureau Spotlight considers it essential to show that this neighbourhood is more than just a collection of social problems, an image that is sometimes reinforced in media coverage.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
WALANDAWE/MOROWALI - A year-long investigation traces nickel from deforested forests and Indigenous land in Sulawesi through China’s battery industry to Volkswagen’s electric cars in Europe, exposing the hidden environmental cost of the green transition.

A year-long investigation traces a nickel supply chain from the forests of Sulawesi, Indonesia, through Chinese refineries and battery manufacturers, to Volkswagen electric vehicles sold across Europe. The reporting centres on the Cahaya and Hengjaya mining concessions, whose output feeds Huayou’s processing operations in Morowali, and examines documented commercial links connecting Huayou to CATL and CATL to Volkswagen.


The investigation combines field reporting with satellite analysis, corporate disclosures and trade records to assess the environmental and social consequences of mining expansion. It finds extensive forest loss linked to nickel extraction, including primary forest and areas of high biodiversity and carbon value. The investigation also documents the impact on the Tolaki Indigenous community, whose traditional livelihoods and collective farmland have been increasingly affected by mining, while a promised local smelter and its expected economic benefits failed to materialise.


At the downstream end, the investigation scrutinises Volkswagen’s claims that its supply chains are protected against deforestation and environmental harm. Volkswagen told reporters it could not rule out that the companies identified might be within its supply chain, but did not disclose specific sourcing arrangements. The investigation does not claim to have physically traced individual nickel molecules into specific battery cells; rather, it establishes a documented chain of commercial and supply relationships linking the mines to Volkswagen through Huayou and CATL. It also raises broader questions about corporate due diligence, supply-chain transparency and the environmental costs of the global transition to electric mobility.

Key findings

  • Nickel mining linked to Volkswagen’s wider supply chain has caused extensive forest loss. TreeMap attributed approximately 1,490 hectares of forest loss within the Cahaya concession since 2001 to nickel mining; at Hengjaya, mining accounted for 772 hectares.
  • The two concessions potentially linked to Volkswagen’s nickel supply chain lost nearly 2,360 hectares of canopy cover, according to the investigation’s analysis.
  • The investigation found a documented supply-chain network linking Cahaya and Hengjaya to Volkswagen through Huayou and CATL. Volkswagen said it could not rule out that the identified companies were in its supply chain.
  • In 2024, Cahaya delivered 11 million tonnes of limonite, almost all of its production, to Huayou’s Morowali smelter; deliveries rose to nearly 12.5 million tonnes in 2025.
  • The investigation documented major environmental risks, including threats to primary forests, high-value carbon sinks and habitat for endangered anoa.
  • The Tolaki community reports losing forests, traditional sources of income and farmland, while the local smelter and development benefits promised in connection with the mining project did not materialise.
  • Volkswagen’s supply-chain controls have significant transparency gaps. The company said it uses satellite monitoring and audits but declined to disclose their results; existing smelter-focused audits do not necessarily establish whether upstream mines are free from deforestation.
  • The investigation raises questions about the climate accounting of EV supply chains, because neither Volkswagen nor its certifier confirmed that emissions from mining-related forest loss were included in the relevant life-cycle assessment.

Methodology

The investigation used a mixed-method, cross-border reporting approach over the course of a year. Reporters conducted on-the-ground interviews and observations in Sulawesi, including with Tolaki community members, local officials, former company personnel, drivers and environmental experts. These findings were combined with satellite and geospatial analysis by specialist organisations, including TreeMap, as well as forest and biodiversity data. The supply chain was reconstructed through corporate annual reports, regulatory filings, shareholder disclosures, official company documents and import-export and shipping records covering principally 2024 and 2025. Reporters cross-checked commercial relationships at successive stages: mining in Cahaya and Hengjaya; processing by Huayou in Indonesia; refining and cathode production in China; battery production by CATL; and deliveries and battery-pack assembly involving Volkswagen. The investigation explicitly distinguishes between documented supply-chain links and physical traceability: no material evidence conclusively proves that nickel from these two mines was incorporated into a specific CATL battery cell shipped to Volkswagen. Companies and relevant authorities were approached for comment, and their responses or refusals to provide details were incorporated into the reporting.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • From Indonesia’s hallowed forests to Volkswagen’s electric cars: the dirty nickel trail, VoxEurop, 16/10/2026
  • Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands, The Guardian, 16/10/2026
  • Dalle foreste dell’Indonesia alle auto elettriche europee: il nichel sporco dietro Volkswagen e Stellantis, Domani, 16/10/2026
  • Wo Urwälder für E-Autos weichen müssen, Süddeutsche Zeitung, 16/10/2026
  • La cara oculta del CUPRA Born: del diseño en Martorell al níquel de Indonesia, InfoLibre, 16/10/2026
  • Voitures électriques : derrière le nickel des batteries, la destruction de la forêt indonésienne, MediaPart, 16/10/2026

COUNTRIES

  • China
  • Germany
  • Indonesia

Team members

Lorenzo di Stasi

Lorenzo Di Stasi is an independent Italian journalist based in Brussels.

James Jackson

James Jackson is a freelance investigative reporter and broadcaster based in Berlin.

Stefano Valentino

Stefano Valentino is a Brussels-based freelance investigative journalist.

Related projects

  • © Pablo Linietsky

    Driving Deforestation. European Luxury Cars' Impact on Indigenous Lands

    ASUNCIÓN - The investigation reveals the links between the European car industry and massive deforestation in Paraguay's Chaco region. It reveals how major luxury car brands such as BMW and Mercedes-Benz buy leather from Italian companies, which in turn source the material from Paraguayan companies involved in illegal deforestation, particularly in the Ayoreo indigenous territories.

    Meer lezen
  • © Marta Abbà

    Italy's Timber Appetite Fuels Albania's Forests Crisis

    TIRANA/MILANO - The destruction of the Balkans' forests continues, especially in the remote areas of Albania where the law doesn't reach and corruption reigns. It's a deep-rooted and local phenomenon, but it's supported by an international dynamic that involves Europe and, above all, the country's best partner in crime: Italy.

    Meer lezen
  • (c) Aqwam Hanifan / Narasi

    #DirtyNickel: Inside The World's Largest Nickel Mine in Indonesia

    JAKARTA – This investigation reveals serious irregularities and testimonies of environmental and social fraud at the Weda Bay Nickel, the world's largest open pit nickel mine, co-owned by the French mining giant Eramet, the Chinese steel multinational Tsinghan and the Indonesian state through the state-owned company PT Antam.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
OSTRAVA – To address the lack of in-depth regional coverage in the Moravian-Silesian Region, Okraj.cz launched the Local Lens project to cultivate a new generation of local journalists. Through an intensive mentoring programme, three young reporters published investigative features on overlooked national minorities, produced podcasts, and hosted public discussions. 

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

The initiative directly enriched the local information ecosystem, giving a platform to underrepresented communities while strengthening the publication's long-term capacity to cover regional news deserts.

Project Activities

Between September 2025 and May 2026, Okraj.cz implemented a comprehensive capacity-building initiative for three selected journalism interns: Barbora, Vojtěch, and Natálie. Paired with personal mentors, the interns participated in an intensive editorial bootcamp in Krnov, featuring tailored workshops on local ethics and in-depth reporting, as well as an expert session on local media environments led by Masaryk University academic Lenka Waschková Císařová.

Throughout the programme, the interns engaged in multi-format reporting, ranging from quick-response news for the "Week in the Region" format to covering local municipal council meetings. The core of their work focused on producing three major long-form investigative features on ethnic minorities in the region, exploring Greek identity, Polish cross-border healthcare dynamics, and German cultural heritage in Hlučínsko. Enhanced by professional photography by Kateřina Šimečková and illustrations by Tereza Ignácová, the project also produced dedicated podcast episodes and culminated in May 2026 with a public panel discussion titled "Moravian-Silesia Among Nations."

What is the impact?

The Local Lens project directly tackled the phenomenon of regional news deserts by injecting fresh, professional editorial resources into the Moravian-Silesian Region. By training and mentoring early-career journalists, the initiative built sustainable local media capacity rather than providing a temporary patch. The long-term impact is evidenced by two of the three interns transitioning into permanent editorial positions at Okraj.cz, ensuring that the region retains skilled reporters dedicated to scrutinising local government and covering underserved topics. Furthermore, the systematic framework created during the PM4D grant period served as a model that successfully attracted follow-up funding from the Endowment Fund for Independent Journalism (NFNŽ) and the Daniel Anýž Fund, securing the newsroom's ongoing presence in the area.

The project brought significantly greater visibility to historically marginalised or overlooked communities within the region, specifically the local Greek, Polish, and German minorities. By moving beyond surface-level reporting to explore complex topics like cross-border healthcare and regional identity, Okraj.cz provided its readership with nuanced, contextual local journalism. Beyond written coverage, the project fostered direct civic engagement through its public panel discussion, "Moravian-Silesia Among Nations," creating a physical space for dialogue between community members, journalists, and local stakeholders.

Project Links

  • Articles / Features 02
  • Articles / Features 03
  • Podcast

Project Pictures

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
EU - Despite EU water laws, this summer the drinking water supply system showed serious cracks in several regions in the European Union. Good water governance and its enforcement are essential to safeguard the access to clean drinking water on our continent. The European Commission is stepping up its efforts to safeguard access to clean and healthy drinking water in the near future, but the road ahead will be winding.

How can persistent drinking water problems remain while new ones are popping up everywhere in Europe, when appropriate European water laws are in place? After investigating real-life situations in several European Member States, the answers are obvious. There is a lack of good water governance, trustworthy data and adequate enforcement, and the sector is facing a serious investment gap. All these things can be addressed, but this needs to be done quickly, because reversing these kind of developments will be hard, if not impossible.

Key Findings

The team of journalists investigated five cases in different Member States, and the results are sometimes quite shocking. In Spain drinking water pollution by livestock farms is a big problem. It leaves many villages without safe and healthy drinking water. In Abruzzo more than half of its water is lost through old, never-replaced networks, while some areas go without water for days. “I shower down at the sea, because I know at home I can’t”, says one on the inhabitants.

In a water-rich country such as The Netherlands the drinking water supply system needs to change drastically. The national government needs to take the lead and start changing national laws to safeguard drinking water in the near future. In Sweden tensions are running high about drinking water prices due to the country’s aging water treatment infrastructure. In Ireland the drinking water supply of the city of Dublin is at stake due to failing infrastructure.

Methodology

The cross-border investigation combined desk research, field reporting and interviews across the countries examined. The journalists conducted interviews in person, online and by email and visited selected regions to document local water challenges and infrastructure.

The team also held regular cross-border meetings to compare findings, identify common patterns and develop new reporting angles.

Water-law expert Marleen van Rijswick provided legal guidance throughout the investigation and reviewed the articles to assess their interpretation of relevant European and national water legislation.

Themes

  • Environment
  • Healthcare

Publication

ONLINE

  • Nelle falle del sistema: il paradosso di una terra ricca d’acqua, Prismag, 01/10/2026
  • Vattnets pris behöver räknas om, Cirkulation, 01/10/2026
  • Wetswijzigingen nodig om Nederlands drinkwater veilig te stellen, H2O Water Network, 08/10/2026

    BRUSSELS – Asbestos is now banned in 69 countries, but it is still found in our drinking water. Water pipes are made of asbestos cement release fibres that can be lethal when inhaled. Experts have warned about this problem for decades, but the issue persists.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
CROATIA / ITALY - This investigation looks at how beaches in Italy and Croatia continue to receive the prestigious Blue Flag certification despite persistent failures to comply with EU wastewater treatment standards.

Every summer, the Blue Flag tells beachgoers that a beach meets strict environmental standards, and one of the scheme’s criteria is that urban wastewater is properly treated. Yet Italy is among the worst performers in the European Union under the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive. The EU Court of Justice has condemned it repeatedly, and it paid more than €210 million in penalties by the end of 2024. Croatia, on the other side of the Adriatic, is also still far from compliance. The Dirty Adriatic asks how the two are able to coexist: how can a certification that guarantees clean water be awarded along coastlines where the public record says wastewater is not properly collected or treated?

The investigation compares official record systems that normally never meet. These are the countries’ own reporting to the European Union on wastewater collection and treatment, the Blue Flag lists and awarding rules, rulings by the EU Court of Justice, and independent bathing-water sampling. It then follows the money and the paperwork behind the certification: who pays for it, with which public funds, and which documents municipalities submit to obtain it. The story comes at a turning point. From 27 September 2026, EU Directive 2024/825 on green claims tightens the rules on sustainability labels and environmental claims presented to consumers.

Methodologically, the team rebuilt Italy’s national submissions under the directive across several reporting cycles and linked them spatially to Blue Flag sites. The findings show inconsistencies and overlaps between official sources, not causal claims. They are backed by around twenty freedom-of-information requests to municipalities, regions, and environmental agencies, municipal administrative records, and field reporting on the Italian and Croatian coasts.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Spiagge Bandiere Blu, il mistero delle procedure e le anomalie nella selezione dei luoghi, Domani, 12/10/2026

    Varna's Hazardous Seafood Exports Throughout Europe

    VARNA - Improper management of a wastewater treatment pipe in the Varna lake has led to repeated toxic leaks since 2019.

    PRESPA LAKE – Prespa lake in North Macedonia is considered even older than the "official" oldest lake in Europe, Ohrid Lake. And it is under threat.

    BUCHAREST - For almost 9 years, Romania has been criticised and monitored by the European Commission for allowing the large-scale destruction of several mountain rivers for the purpose of building micro-hydropower plants, without complying with the Water Framework and Habitats Directives.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
MILAN / WARSAW / KYIV - How Europe's exceptional welcome of 2022 turned into years of permanent uncertainty, exposing the cracks of a reception system that expects people in need to accept whatever they are offered.

The arrival of millions of Ukrainians in 2022 is remembered as a unique act of European solidarity, and it was one. For the first time, temporary protection was activated, and people fleeing the war received legal status, the right to work, healthcare and freedom of movement almost overnight. In Italy, around 170,000 people found shelter, mostly in the homes of relatives, the long-established Ukrainian community and Italian families who opened their doors within days. In Poland, a country more used to sending people abroad than receiving them, an emergency law gave refugees equal access to healthcare and child benefits, and civil society took in hundreds of thousands of people.

This story also has a darker side. More than four years later, the emergency has not ended, and protection that was meant to be temporary has become a permanent state of uncertainty. Permits are still renewed one year at a time, now up to March 2028. Every extension or legal change arrives late and unpredictably, and none of these years count towards a lasting status. Many refugees, for their part, still live with a suspended migration project. They did not choose to leave, they see their stay as a pause, and they put off learning the language or planning a future, because giving up on return feels like a surrender.

Key Findings

  • Prolonged temporariness has shown what happens when a status built for a short emergency is stretched over years. Every renewal puts access to healthcare, family benefits and housing at risk, and every announced legal change sends people rushing to offices to secure their rights. Bureaucracy creates closed circles. Without a registered address there is no ID, without ID there is no bank account, and without a bank account a person with a job cannot be paid. Welfare and social housing schemes require permits or years of residence that a one-year status can never provide. The new routes to longer-term permits reward those with stable contracts and leave the elderly, carers and single mothers behind. As collective accommodation closes, some people fall into homelessness, including men sent back from other EU countries.
  • The assumption that people who arrive in need, and who are foreigners, should accept whatever they are offered. The investigation found it at every step. Many people end up in informal sublets, and some are asked by agents for upfront fees. Landlords demand deposits worth several months of rent, hang up when they hear a foreign accent, or blame a whole nationality for one tenant's damage. Doctors, engineers and pharmacists clean houses because recognising a diploma is costly and slow. Some employers expect gratitude and silence instead of fair pay. Those who ask questions or claim their rights are quickly labelled demanding. The Ukrainian experience makes visible a mindset that weighs on everyone who depends on the reception system.
  • Scattered across both countries, there are also examples of good integration. They tend to appear where the local community plays an active part and where a Ukrainian community was already present: parishes, local associations, Caritas networks, diaspora organisations and families who stayed by people's side for years. Most households have at least one member in regular work, and many have rebuilt a fragile stability. These successes, however, depend on goodwill rather than on the system. Volunteer support faded within one or two years, public attention dropped, and in both countries political tensions, sensationalist media and disinformation eroded the early solidarity. The system keeps confirming and perpetuating the mechanisms that weigh on refugees' future and on their mental health. Living from one deadline to the next creates constant anxiety. People cannot plan six months ahead, and many spend years in reception facilities, losing hope without gaining a plan. Families are split by conscription rules, and some parents have not seen their children for years. Many grieve the professional identity they built at home. Everyday hostility, online attacks and a silence that keeps most victims from reporting abuse add fear to uncertainty.

Methodology

The project brings together a team working in Italy, Poland and Ukraine and uses the same method in both host countries. For more than six months, the team conducted in-depth interviews with researchers, reception coordinators, social workers, cultural mediators, housing specialists, civic activists and psychologists, and gathered personal testimonies separately from refugees of different ages and backgrounds. In Italy, fieldwork covered Lombardy, Veneto and Trentino. In Poland, interviews were combined with a mystery-call investigation of the rental market in six cities. The research was also enriched by a conversation with project advisor Nellija Locmele, who provided an additional perspective on the issues explored. Interviews with Ukrainian and European experts on migration policy, return prospects and integration indicators frame both national cases.

Themes

  • Armed conflict
  • Migration
  • Social affairs

Publication

ONLINE

  • Le vite sospese dei rifugiati ucraini in Europa, OBCT, 08/10/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Ukraine
  • Poland

Marta Abbà is an investigative journalists based in Milan.

The new routes to longer-term permits reward those with stable contracts and leave the elderly, carers and single mothers behind. As collective accommodation closes, some people fall into homelessness, including men sent back from other EU countries.
  • The assumption that people who arrive in need, and who are foreigners, should accept whatever they are offered. The investigation found it at every step. Many people end up in informal sublets, and some are asked by agents for upfront fees. Landlords demand deposits worth several months of rent, hang up when they hear a foreign accent, or blame a whole nationality for one tenant's damage. Doctors, engineers and pharmacists clean houses because recognising a diploma is costly and slow. Some employers expect gratitude and silence instead of fair pay. Those who ask questions or claim their rights are quickly labelled demanding. The Ukrainian experience makes visible a mindset that weighs on everyone who depends on the reception system.
  • Scattered across both countries, there are also examples of good integration. They tend to appear where the local community plays an active part and where a Ukrainian community was already present: parishes, local associations, Caritas networks, diaspora organisations and families who stayed by people's side for years. Most households have at least one member in regular work, and many have rebuilt a fragile stability. These successes, however, depend on goodwill rather than on the system. Volunteer support faded within one or two years, public attention dropped, and in both countries political tensions, sensationalist media and disinformation eroded the early solidarity. The system keeps confirming and perpetuating the mechanisms that weigh on refugees' future and on their mental health. Living from one deadline to the next creates constant anxiety. People cannot plan six months ahead, and many spend years in reception facilities, losing hope without gaining a plan. Families are split by conscription rules, and some parents have not seen their children for years. Many grieve the professional identity they built at home. Everyday hostility, online attacks and a silence that keeps most victims from reporting abuse add fear to uncertainty.

Methodology

The project brings together a team working in Italy, Poland and Ukraine and uses the same method in both host countries. For more than six months, the team conducted in-depth interviews with researchers, reception coordinators, social workers, cultural mediators, housing specialists, civic activists and psychologists, and gathered personal testimonies separately from refugees of different ages and backgrounds. In Italy, fieldwork covered Lombardy, Veneto and Trentino. In Poland, interviews were combined with a mystery-call investigation of the rental market in six cities. The research was also enriched by a conversation with project advisor Nellija Locmele, who provided an additional perspective on the issues explored. Interviews with Ukrainian and European experts on migration policy, return prospects and integration indicators frame both national cases.

item.description:
BUDAPEST - Flavescence dorée, a devastating grapevine disease, is spreading across Central Europe, threatening vineyards and the livelihoods of winegrowers.

The team's cross-border investigation examines how a threat identified by scientists years ago developed into a major epidemic – and why institutions failed to respond effectively while there was still time to contain it.

The team investigates what authorities in Hungary, Austria, and Romania knew about the disease, when they knew it, and what measures they took – or failed to take. The reporting looks at the capacity of authorities to monitor and contain the outbreak, gaps in surveillance and laboratory testing, the role of neglected and abandoned vineyards, and the incentives that may discourage growers from reporting infections.

The investigation also explores how climate change is contributing to the spread of the insect that transmits the disease, and how different approaches among winegrowers – from conventional chemical treatment to organic and more holistic practices – shape the response.

By comparing three countries at different stages of the epidemic, the project aims to identify the institutional and practical failures that allowed the crisis to escalate, as well as lessons that could help Romania and other countries prepare before the disease becomes even more widespread.

Methodology

The investigation combines cross-border investigative reporting, Freedom of Information requests, documentary research, scientific interviews and field reporting. The teams in Hungary, Austria and Romania are examining official records, surveillance and inspection data, legislation, institutional correspondence and government decisions, while interviewing scientists, winegrowers, industry representatives, officials and other relevant sources.

The three-country comparison is central to the methodology: rather than examining the outbreak in isolation, the team traces what authorities knew and did over time and compares institutional capacity, enforcement, reporting mechanisms and responses across countries at different stages of the epidemic.

Field reporting and audiovisual interviews are used to document the experiences of affected winegrowers and connect the institutional findings to the human and economic consequences of the disease.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
SAN PETERSBURG / ALESSANDRIA - Chemicals made in Russia keep crossing the EU to reach an Italian plant, despite the war in Ukraine and years of sanctions. Middlemen in Germany and Israel, trucks through Estonia and a price that rose eightfold kept the supply going.

Since February 2022, the European Union has adopted package after package of sanctions to cut trade with Russia. Yet one Russian-made chemical has kept travelling across Europe to a factory near Alessandria, in northern Italy.

The substance is 8-CNVE, a PFAS monomer used to make heat-resistant rubbers for aerospace seals and military vehicles. It is produced in St Petersburg by Anles, a company owned by the Kogan family and, according to import records, the only producer of this compound in the world. Its buyer in Italy is Syensqo, formerly Solvay, at its Spinetta Marengo plant.

The route is long and deliberately layered. The chemical leaves Russia in specialised leased containers, enters the EU through Estonia, crosses the continent by road and is sold through an intermediary: first Ftoran, registered at a private house in Birkenau, Germany, and from September 2022 Elastofluor, based in Israel.

The war did not stop the supply. From autumn 2023 the price of 8-CNVE exported to Europe rose to eight times its earlier level, a sign of a shrinking and riskier market, but Syensqo kept buying. In July, new EU sanctions targeting nitriles brought this kind of trade directly into question.

Across three episodes, this investigation reconstructs the supply chain, asks who knew where the chemical came from, and examines what companies along the route, and Italy itself, now risk.

Key findings

  • A PFAS monomer produced only in Russia, 8-CNVE, continued to reach Syensqo's plant in Alessandria after the invasion of Ukraine.
  • Shipments enter the EU through Estonia and cross Europe by road before arriving in Italy.
  • Sales run through intermediaries: Ftoran in Germany, replaced in September 2022 by Elastofluor in Israel.
  • The first recorded shipment to Alessandria dates from November 2021: 200 kg net, worth more than €230,000.
  • From autumn 2023 the export price to Europe rose up to eightfold, yet Syensqo continued to buy.
  • Syensqo registered 8-CNVE with ECHA in 2024 and filed the safety data sheet with local authorities in Alessandria around two years later.
  • New EU sanctions on nitriles, adopted on 25 July, raise questions about the legality of the trade and the responsibility of each company in the chain.

Methodology

The team began with trade data from the Import Genius database, searching shipping records under Anles's Russian company name. These documents list the supplier, buyer, intermediary, quantities, value and country of transit for each consignment. The team then cross-checked them against the ECHA registry, Italian local authority records, company registers in Russia, Germany, Estonia and Israel, and patent filings. The team reviewed confidential emails and carried out field reporting in Birkenau and Heidelberg, Germany, and along the Estonian–Russian border. The team then sent detailed questions to the companies involved, including Anles, Ftoran, Elastofluor, Syensqo, Arcese and Eurotainer, and interviewed experts on sanctions law and EU trade.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • La rotta russa dei pfas: così le sostanze continuano a entrare in Europa, La Via Libera, 05/10/2026
  • Опасный груз: токсичные химикаты просачивались в Италию из России через Эстонию, Деловые Ведомости, 05/10/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • ITALY
  • Russia

Team members

Marta Abbà is an investigative journalists based in Milan.

Laura Fazzini

Laura Fazzini is a freelance journalist based in Milan, Italy.

Ekaterina Mereminskaia

Ekaterina Mereminskaia is a financial and investigative journalist based in Tallinn.

Media

Äripäev is a digital business-news outlet and Estonia's leading financial media.

Emanuele Piano is an Italian award winning investigative journalist presently based in Istanbul, Türkiye.

Related projects

    ANTWERP - The pollution around the 3M plant near Antwerp (Belgium) has been known for years. Yet the PFOS scandal did not erupt in Flanders until the spring of 2021.

    VLADIVOSTOK / BUSAN – After Russia attacked Ukraine, the West acted swiftly. Within months, the Western alliance imposed hard-hitting sanctions against the Eastern giant. However, these sanctions did not affect most Russian fishing industries, which kept exporting 1.1 billion USD of seafood into Europe

item.description:
GALICIA / SANTAREM - A cross-border investigation into how eucalyptus expansion, rural abandonment, economic dependence and difficulties in enforcing forestry rules interact with wildfire risk.

Eucalyptus and Forest Fires Across Galicia and Portugal investigates how the expansion of eucalyptus plantations interacts with a forestry model shaped by rural abandonment, fragmented land ownership, economic dependence and difficulties in enforcing forestry rules. GaliciaPress and O Mirante approached the issue from a cross-border perspective, combining documentary research, field reporting and interviews with academics, scientists, firefighters, landowners, public authorities, environmental organisations and representatives of the forestry and pulp industries.

The reporting shows that wildfire risk cannot be explained by a single factor. Fuel continuity, accumulated biomass, land abandonment, forest management and species composition interact in ways that can intensify fire behaviour and make prevention more difficult. The investigation also examined why restrictions and moratoria do not always translate into effective control on the ground, while documenting the economic reasons that make eucalyptus attractive to many small landowners.

The project also explored alternatives, including collective forest management, diversification with broadleaf species and other rural land-use models intended to combine economic viability with greater resilience to wildfire.

Key Findings

  • Eucalyptus does not explain wildfires on its own. Experts highlighted the combined effect of fuel continuity, accumulated biomass, land abandonment, insufficient management and forest composition.
  • Economic dependence is a central part of the problem. For many small rural landowners, eucalyptus remains one of the few forestry options capable of generating income within a relatively short time frame.
  • The investigation found a gap between forestry regulation and effective enforcement, including difficulties obtaining sanctioning data and monitoring potentially illegal plantations.
  • Galicia and Portugal share structural challenges, including rural depopulation, fragmented ownership, land abandonment and difficulties in forest governance.
  • Alternatives to monoculture exist - including collective management, diversification and other rural land-use models - but scaling them requires organisation, incentives and long-term public policy.

Methodology

The investigation used a cross-border mixed-method approach. GaliciaPress focused primarily on documentary and data research, regulatory analysis, access-to-information requests and interviews with academics, scientists, forestry professionals, public authorities and industry representatives.

O Mirante concentrated strongly on field reporting and the social dimension of the investigation in Portugal, visiting affected territories and interviewing rural residents, landowners, firefighters, local authorities and forestry specialists.

The two newsrooms regularly shared findings and compared evidence from both countries to identify common patterns and differences in forest policy, land ownership, economic incentives and wildfire risk.

    ATHENS/FARO/AGRIGENTO – Wildfires in Europe have become more frequent and devastating. From lagging prevention and disaster response in Greece, to the mismanagement and legal loopholes that in Italy fuel arson, to the post-wildfire economy in Spain that impedes ecological restoration, to Portugal's paper industry that hinder fire management for its own financial gain, this investigation sheds light on the reasons behind these disasters.

    VIGO – Spain and Portugal share their main rivers, a fact that has promoted diplomatic efforts for the joint management of common bodies of water.
