    Meer lezen

    Behind The Flames: Wildfires in Turkey and Italy

    IZMIR / CATANIA – Forest wildfires have increased in size and impact. Every year, 375,000 hectares of land in Mediterranean countries are scorched. Journalists tried to identify the main factors that lead to these disasters, which treaten entire ecosystems.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
LUANDA - A cross-border investigation reveals European, British and US oil giants have been routinely spilling oil in Angola’s oceans for 13 years, leaving residents ill and unable to eat. Multiple complaints have been ignored, while fishermen are asked to clean up under ‘voluntary work agreements’.

While Western oil majors pledge a “zero-spill mindset” at home, a year-long investigation - combining on-the-ground reporting from Zaire and Cabinda, exclusive satellite data, and internal documents - reveals a hidden human and environmental crisis along the Angolan coast.

Exclusive satellite analysis of Block 15 (operated by ExxonMobil, and owned by BP, Eni, Equinor and Sonangol) exposes chronic spills covering an area equivalent to at least the size of Montenegro over the past 13 years, vastly contradicting official state figures. On the ground, field interviews show how routine spills poison essential crops, ruin fisheries, and expose residents to carcinogens and toxic hydrogen sulfide gas. Local fishermen reveal they are informally hired to clean up toxic crude with no formal contracts or health insurance, while behind-the-scenes extrajudicial interference stymies legal accountability.

Supported by original field testimony, legal documents, and unpublished satellite imagery, this investigation lays bare the stark double standards and corporate impunity of Big Oil in West Africa.

Key findings

  • Satellite imagery analysis revealed chronic and unreported oil spills around Angola’s Kizomba A field in Block 15 over 13 years. It is operated by ExxonMobil and co-owned by BP, Eni, Equinor and Sonangol.
  • The size of the spill ranges from a minimum cumulative total of 89538 barrels to a possible 4476908 barrels - nearly as much as BP’s Deepwater Horizon disaster. The range occurs because it is not possible to determine the thickness of the oil without physically testing it.
  • The gap between these figures and official records from Angola and the oil giants is stark. Reporting of spills over one barrel is required by Angolan law, but the national oil and gas agency ANPG reports an average of just 450 spilt barrels a year across every offshore block. Similarly, reporting by the oil giants showed very low figures. All of them have state policies of no harm.
  • Wind and current data analysis suggests a portion of the oil may be travelling to the shore. Residents' testimonies support this, noting severe health and agricultural impacts - although they cannot trace the source of the oil to a single block.
  • Residents and health officials report an increase in skin infections, gastrointestinal distress and nausea from the smell of toxic hydrogen sulfide. Health officials shared registries documenting this. Food and fish are blackened by the oil, but many residents are left without any option but to eat them. Cabinda’s ex-health secretary believes there has been a rise in skin cancer because of exposure to the oil.
  • The availability of fish has also drastically decreased, affecting fishermen’s livelihoods as well as available protein sources.
  • Documents show Chevron asked fishermen to clean up a spill under ‘voluntary work agreements’. Workers were given basic rubber boots, gloves and masks, but no formal contracts and no insurance. One ambulance was kept on standby, they reported. They added that this incident was indicative of clean-ups for bigger spills in general across the coast.
  • At least 13 countries worldwide benefit from the oil, including China, India, the United States, Canada, Spain, and Italy. More than 370 million barrels of oil have been shipped to refineries and installations. The chain has links with some controversial entities, such as Trafigura and Glencore as charterers. TotalEnergies, Shell, ConocoPhillips, Sinopec and Sinochem have also acted as charterers, while Sinopec, IOC, Sinochem, Nayara Energy, Repsol and Petronas have bought from the block.

Methodology

This investigation combined open-source and data journalism with on-the-ground reporting.

The team analysed satellite imagery, literature and expert testimony to assess oil spills and their environmental impact. Trade data, ship tracking, corporate records and regulatory research were used to trace the oil, identify companies involved and examine legal and reporting obligations.

Over the course of a year, the team built relationships with Angolan residents and experts before reporting from affected communities along the coast. This included interviews, photo and video documention, access to health records and closed-source legal documents.

The team worked with a whistleblower organisation to ensure informed consent, and protected identities where necessary for safety.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Oil giants’ systematic spills are poisoning Angola’s coast and its communities, Voxeurop, 28/09/2026
  • “Quelle” del blocco 15, il petrolio a perdere che avvelena l’Angola, Domani, 28/09/2026
  • Os derrames sistemáticos das gigantes petrolíferas estão a envenenar a costa de Angola e as suas comunidades, Expresso, 28/09/2026

more to come

COUNTRIES

  • Angola
  • Italy
  • United Kingdom

Team members

Giorgio Michalopoulos

Giorgio Michalopoulos is an Italian journalist based in Brazil.

Stéffie Banatvala

Stéffie Banatvala is a Parsi, British and French freelance investigative journalist.

Mentors

Sam Leon

Sam Leon (London) is a data investigator with experience in both journalism and policy.

Related projects

  • © Ekpali Saint

    The Impact of ENI’s Extractivism in Italy and Nigeria

    IKEBIRI / POTENZA - From the dry hills of southern Italy's Basilicata region to the flood-stricken communities of Nigeria’s Niger Delta, oil giant Eni has left a trail of pollution and environmental degradation spanning continents. This cross-border investigation examines the consequences.

    Meer lezen
  • ©Danil Usmanov

    Kazakhstan: The Cost of Oil

    ATYRAU - As the EU deepens its energy partnership with Kazakhstan, this investigation goes to the source of the oil that helps power European markets. Reporting from Atyrau, Kazakhstan's oil capital, it explores the social and environmental costs of decades of oil extraction.

    Meer lezen

  • The Disappearance of Prespa Lake

    PRESPA LAKE – Prespa lake in North Macedonia is considered even older than the "official" oldest lake in Europe, Ohrid Lake. And it is under threat.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
GENEVA - The IPCC is one of the most respected scientific institutions in climate research. An investigation into its inner workings now reveals strong links to the Saudi government within its ranks, as well as apparent contradictions of the IPCC’s application of its conflict of interest rules.

The IPCC is the world’s most authoritative international body on climate science. Its reports underpin UN climate negotiations and inform national climate policy around the world. Yet, its conflict of interest policy is described by experts as failing.

This investigation reveals the growing presence of Saudi Arabia, the world's second-largest oil producer, within the IPCC, and present more than 20 cases with significant conflict-of-interest concerns from among the authors selected for their upcoming 7th Assessment Report.

Having done background checks for over 200 IPCC authors, the team identified major problems with both the design and application of the organization’s conflict of interest policy, an analysis backed by experts and former IPCC authors.

Key findings

  • At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests. An IPCC vice-chair is also employed by the Saudi energy ministry.
  • The IPCC’s conflict of interest policy is described by experts as failing and this investigation has found discrepancies between what the policy says and the findings on the background checks of about 20 authors of the upcoming 7th Assessment Report.

Methodology

The investigation is based on background checks of 223 authors of the IPCC’s Working Group III for the upcoming 7th Assessment Report. After a thorough search of the authors’ profiles, the team presented its findings to two independent reviewers, as well as to former IPCC authors and experts in several relevant fields. The conflicts of interest were grouped according to their nature and the team has put the list through several rounds of verification until they achieved the final number.

Themes

  • Climate

Publication

ONLINE

  • How Saudi oil scientists ended up working on the world’s most important climate reports, The Guardian, 21/09/2026
  • Conflits d’intérêts au GIEC : comment l’Arabie saoudite et Aramco ont infiltré le prochain rapport, l'Humanité, 21/09/2026
  • Abbiamo scoperto dei conflitti d’interesse dentro all’IPCC. C’entra il petrolio saudita, Lucy Sui Mondi, 21/09/2026
  • Cómo expertos de la gran petrolera saudí se colaron como autores de los informes climáticos más importantes del mundo, El diario, 21/09/2026

VIDEO

  • Wie unabhängig berichtet der Weltklimarat?, 3Sat, 21/09/2026

FOLLOW-UP

  • Ölexperten aus Saudiarabien arbeiten an zentralem UNO-Klimabericht mit, Tages-Anzeiger, 21/09/2026

GENEVA - The IPCC is one of the most respected scientific institutions in climate research. An investigation into its inner workings now reveals strong links to the Saudi government within its ranks, as well as apparent contradictions of the IPCC’s application of its conflict of interest rules.

The IPCC is the world’s most authoritative international body on climate science. Its reports underpin UN climate negotiations and inform national climate policy around the world. Yet, its conflict of interest policy is described by experts as failing.

This investigation reveals the growing presence of Saudi Arabia, the world's second-largest oil producer, within the IPCC, and present more than 20 cases with significant conflict-of-interest concerns from among the authors selected for their upcoming 7th Assessment Report.

Having done background checks for over 200 IPCC authors, the team identified major problems with both the design and application of the organization’s conflict of interest policy, an analysis backed by experts and former IPCC authors.

Key findings

  • At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests. An IPCC vice-chair is also employed by the Saudi energy ministry.
  • The IPCC’s conflict of interest policy is described by experts as failing and this investigation has found discrepancies between what the policy says and the findings on the background checks of about 20 authors of the upcoming 7th Assessment Report.

Methodology

The investigation is based on background checks of 223 authors of the IPCC’s Working Group III for the upcoming 7th Assessment Report. After a thorough search of the authors’ profiles, the team presented its findings to two independent reviewers, as well as to former IPCC authors and experts in several relevant fields. The conflicts of interest were grouped according to their nature and the team has put the list through several rounds of verification until they achieved the final number.

Themes

  • Climate

Publication

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
PUERTOLLANO/VENICE/NAPAJEDLA/MUNICH -Sold as a green industrial revolution, Europe's hydrogen valleys are increasingly a story about lobbying, import dependency and who controls the pipes.

Europe's hydrogen strategy was pitched as a local industrial revival: clean fuel, made and used close to home, replacing fossil imports with homegrown green molecules. Four years on, that vision has quietly shifted into something more geopolitical. Governments and incumbents are re-routing the narrative towards imports, pipeline repurposing and long-distance corridors, while the companies best placed to benefit are the same gas and energy majors that dominated the fossil era, repositioned as the indispensable infrastructure operators of the "green" one.

In Germany, regulatory uncertainty is prompting even funded projects to walk away from public money, while industry consolidates around new lobbying blocs pressing collectively for more state backing, a sign that the sector's centre of gravity is shifting from many small players to a handful of large ones. In Spain and the Czech Republic, the gap between political ambition and delivered infrastructure is exposed by cancelled projects and contested job claims, revealing how easily industrial promises outpace reality on the ground, and how local communities are left to weigh the costs - land, water, disrupted ecosystems - against benefits that often fail to materialise. In Italy, national policy has pivoted from local production to positioning the country as a transit hub between North Africa and Central Europe, keeping legacy gas infrastructure, and its operators, relevant for another generation rather than displacing them.

Across all four countries, the same pattern recurs: hydrogen infrastructure is increasingly shaped to serve strategic and political interests rather than proven industrial demand, with incumbents using the transition to entrench, not disrupt, their position - and public subsidy acting less as a bridge to a new market than as a lifeline for the old one.

Key findings

  • European hydrogen policy is drifting from local, demand-led production towards geopolitical positioning - securing import routes and transit status over genuine domestic capacity.
  • In Germany, funded projects are being abandoned over regulatory uncertainty even as incumbents form new lobbying alliances for further state support.
  • National ambition is being quietly scaled back in several countries, with targets loosened well behind original goals.
  • Flagship projects in Spain and the Czech Republic have met local resistance or outright failure, undercutting the narrative of a smooth, job-creating transition.
  • In Italy, strategy has shifted from local valleys to positioning the country as an indispensable transit corridor, keeping existing gas infrastructure central to the "green" transition.
  • Incumbent players repeatedly occupy dual roles as both lobbyists and beneficiaries of the funding rules they help shape - a structural conflict of interest across several countries examined.

Methodology

Findings combine desk research into EU and national funding frameworks and project registries with original interviews across the four countries - company spokespeople, industry associations, local officials and environmental groups. Claims about project status were cross-checked against multiple independent sources where possible, including site-level reporting and official documentation.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Idrogeno verde, la grande illusione europea, La Via Libera, 15/09/2026
  • Puertollano busca en el hidrógeno su próxima transición industrial, Climatica, 16/09/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Czech Republic
  • Germany
  • Italy
  • Spain

Team members

Marta Abbà

Marta Abbà is an investigative journalists based in Milan.

Fermín Grodira

Fermín Grodira is an investigative journalists based in Spain.

Mayya Chernobylskaya

Mayya Chernobylskaya is a freelance journalist based in Germany.

Martin Vrba

Martin Vrba is an independent Czech journalist and essayist.

Laura Fazzini

Laura Fazzini is a freelance journalist based in Milan, Italy.

Related projects

  • © Marcos Garcia Rey

    The Chlorpyrifos Case

    BRUSSELS - Residues of Chlorpyrifos, a dangerous insecticide, have been found in fruit baskets and samples of human urine across Europe. This large, cross-border investigation unveils its risks for the public. 

    Meer lezen
  • © Olivia Acland

    Manganese: Green for Europe, Toxic for Georgia

    CHIATURA –  Georgia is a key supplier of manganese, an essential raw material for Europe’s transition to renewable energy which is used in wind turbines and electric cars. This investigation  shows how the EU's rush to secure critical raw materials for its green transition is colliding with weak environmental oversight, opaque corporate networks, and a dramatically shrinking civic space in Georgia.

    Meer lezen
  • © Francesco Pistilli

    Geothermal Divide: Green Ambitions Meet Local Realities

    BIHOR/RADICOFANI - Produced by tapping into the heat stored beneath the Earth’s surface, geothermal energy is regarded as one of the most promising renewable sources, with a largely untapped potential. This investigation explores the different experiences local communities across Europe have with this energy source. 

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BUCHAREST / SARAJEVO - Mega hydropower projects conceived decades ago during the communist era are now being resumed and developed, ignoring current priorities for water, biodiversity protection, and public spending.

Dams of the Past, Costs of the Present is a cross-border investigation into large hydropower projects in Romania and Bosnia & Herzegovina. First conceived during the communist era (before 1990) they were resumed in recent years, without taking into account technological developments, climate change and in areas that have meanwhile acquired a biodiversity protection regime, with different economic, social and environmental challenges. Despite criticism from experts and opposition from local communities and environmental activists, the projects are moving forward due to the financial interests and political connections behind them.

In Bosnia & Herzegovina, the investigation focuses on the Upper Horizons hydropower scheme, which diverts water through the complex karst system of eastern Herzegovina for electricity production, potentially affecting the Neretva basin and its tributaries to the Adriatic Sea.

In Romania, the projects on the Jiu (Bumbești-Livezeni), Bâsca Mare (Surduc-Siriu) and Răstolița rivers were investigated in particular, because they affect several national parks and Natura 2000 sites, as well as the communities that depend on them.

Together, the cases and stories ask a central question: why are these projects being resumed now, especially given their outstanding financial cost and environmental damage, compared to existing alternatives (wind, solar and battery storage)?

Key findings

  • The Upper Horizons system (Bosnia & Herzegovina) will permanently redistribute water through one of the most complex karst areas in Europe, with potential consequences for the Buna, Bunica and Bregava rivers and the wider Neretva basin. Scientists and environmental groups warn that reduced freshwater flows could increase pressure on ecosystems, endemic species, agriculture and downstream communities, including the Neretva delta in Croatia.
  • The Bumbești-Livezeni project (Romania) involves the capture and dewatering of approximately 30 kilometres of the Jiu River, which is a defining and essential part of the Jiu Gorge National Park. The Răstolița project (Romania) affects the Călimani National Park, a Natura 2000 site, and other protected areas downstream on the Mureș River. The Bâsca Mare dam (Romania), also a piped diversion project (like the Jiu dam), risks leaving a community with several thousand inhabitants who depend on it without water (drinking water, agriculture, livestock farming, tourism).
  • Romania’s energy crisis during summer 2026, was caused by historical minimum flows of the Danube and inland rivers. This confirmed the warnings expressed by specialists, according to which the projects in question will be useless (due to the lack of water) and will not ensure even the expected marginal contribution (less than 1%) to the national energy system. The remaining amounts spent (approximately 450 million euros, only in the case of the three projects investigated) would be sufficient for the installation of solar panels and storage batteries with an installed capacity several times higher.
  • However, in Bosnia & Herzegovina as well as Romania, the development of the projects are moving forward despite disputes over their environmental impact and calls for a reassessment based on contemporary scientific knowledge and climate conditions.
  • Hundreds of millions of euros are involved in the construction and financing of these projects, while questions remain about transparency, public oversight and the long-term financial risks borne by public institutions and companies with majority state capital.
  • The investigation reveals a fundamental conflict between policymakers who present hydropower projects as strategic energy infrastructure and scientists, environmental organizations and affected communities who argue that the half-baked projects need to be reassessed both economically and socially, and above all, before their environmental consequences become irreversible.

Methodology

The investigation combines field reporting, interviews, requests for information and public positions, participation in parliamentary debates, analysis of documents and open source information (OSINT), and cross-border collaboration between journalists from Romania and Bosnia & Herzegovina. Reporters visited the areas affected by the hydropower projects and interviewed local residents, scientists, representatives of civic organizations (local and/or environmental), government representatives, lawyers, public officials, and experts in water engineering, biodiversity, energy and public finance.

Findings from the two countries were compared to identify common patterns in the implementation of hydropower projects conceived decades ago, under fundamentally different environmental, political, and economic conditions.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Gornji horizonti: Projekat iz prošlog vijeka mijenja budućnost Neretve, detektor.ba, 19/09/2026
  • Gornji horizonti: Projekat iz prošlog vijeka mijenja budućnost Neretve, guerila info, 20/09/2026

More to come

FOLLOW UP

  • Romania

Related projects

  • Small Hydropower Plants Causing Big Damage to Rivers in BiH

    SARAJEVO - This investigation explores the damages caused to nature and small rural communities by the construction of the small hydropower plants and their access roads, and what drove investors, especially foreign ones, to seek opportunities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

    Meer lezen

    The Costs of 'Green' Hydropower and Poor River Management

    OSIJEK – Mura-Drava-Danube is a UNESCO-protected biosphere reserve. It spans over 300,000 ha and includes more than 700 km of connected rivers. This investigation reveals poor management practices, lack of cooperation between five national governments, and lack of conservation efforts.

    Meer lezen

    Climate Change and Mismanagement Deplete Water Reserves in Europe

    BARUTH / ORTONA / TÂRGU NEAMȚ - Across Europe, communities are facing a water crisis fueled by decades of poor groundwater management and climate change. This investigation examines the causes and consequences of water scarcity related to groundwater reserves in three of the most affected EU countries: Italy, Germany, and Romania.

Despite criticism from experts and opposition from local communities and environmental activists, the projects are moving forward due to the financial interests and political connections behind them.

In Bosnia & Herzegovina, the investigation focuses on the Upper Horizons hydropower scheme, which diverts water through the complex karst system of eastern Herzegovina for electricity production, potentially affecting the Neretva basin and its tributaries to the Adriatic Sea.

In Romania, the projects on the Jiu (Bumbești-Livezeni), Bâsca Mare (Surduc-Siriu) and Răstolița rivers were investigated in particular, because they affect several national parks and Natura 2000 sites, as well as the communities that depend on them.

Together, the cases and stories ask a central question: why are these projects being resumed now, especially given their outstanding financial cost and environmental damage, compared to existing alternatives (wind, solar and battery storage)?

Key findings

  • The Upper Horizons system (Bosnia & Herzegovina) will permanently redistribute water through one of the most complex karst areas in Europe, with potential consequences for the Buna, Bunica and Bregava rivers and the wider Neretva basin. Scientists and environmental groups warn that reduced freshwater flows could increase pressure on ecosystems, endemic species, agriculture and downstream communities, including the Neretva delta in Croatia.
  • The Bumbești-Livezeni project (Romania) involves the capture and dewatering of approximately 30 kilometres of the Jiu River, which is a defining and essential part of the Jiu Gorge National Park. The Răstolița project (Romania) affects the Călimani National Park, a Natura 2000 site, and other protected areas downstream on the Mureș River. The Bâsca Mare dam (Romania), also a piped diversion project (like the Jiu dam), risks leaving a community with several thousand inhabitants who depend on it without water (drinking water, agriculture, livestock farming, tourism).
  • Romania’s energy crisis during summer 2026, was caused by historical minimum flows of the Danube and inland rivers. This confirmed the warnings expressed by specialists, according to which the projects in question will be useless (due to the lack of water) and will not ensure even the expected marginal contribution (less than 1%) to the national energy system. The remaining amounts spent (approximately 450 million euros, only in the case of the three projects investigated) would be sufficient for the installation of solar panels and storage batteries with an installed capacity several times higher.
  • However, in Bosnia & Herzegovina as well as Romania, the development of the projects are moving forward despite disputes over their environmental impact and calls for a reassessment based on contemporary scientific knowledge and climate conditions.
  • Hundreds of millions of euros are involved in the construction and financing of these projects, while questions remain about transparency, public oversight and the long-term financial risks borne by public institutions and companies with majority state capital.
  • The investigation reveals a fundamental conflict between policymakers who present hydropower projects as strategic energy infrastructure and scientists, environmental organizations and affected communities who argue that the half-baked projects need to be reassessed both economically and socially, and above all, before their environmental consequences become irreversible.

Methodology

The investigation combines field reporting, interviews, requests for information and public positions, participation in parliamentary debates, analysis of documents and open source information (OSINT), and cross-border collaboration between journalists from Romania and Bosnia & Herzegovina. Reporters visited the areas affected by the hydropower projects and interviewed local residents, scientists, representatives of civic organizations (local and/or environmental), government representatives, lawyers, public officials, and experts in water engineering, biodiversity, energy and public finance.

Findings from the two countries were compared to identify common patterns in the implementation of hydropower projects conceived decades ago, under fundamentally different environmental, political, and economic conditions.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BRUSSELS / RIBERALTA - From Brussels to Riberalta, the ‘pearl of the Bolivian Amazon’. An investigation into the European frontier of green finance: the carbon credit market is targeting Bolivia’s indigenous territories, whose rights are at risk of being trampled on. One controversial project shows the dangers involved to frontline communities.

In the heart of the Amazon rainforest in Bolivia, home to more than 30 indigenous communities, Indigenous leaders are currently fighting to defend their territories and natural resources from European and global green policy measures, promoted as a solution to climate change. The EU has recently allowed for carbon credits to make up part of its emissions targets for 2050, accelerating already growing demand for credit, mostly generated in the Global South. In Bolivia, the EU has facilitated the opening of a new market for credits, mainly from forest protection programmes in the Amazon. But one such project, led by a Bolivian politician whose foundation planned to sell credits, was torn up after affected indigenous groups claimed they had been misled and exploited. Through this project, which indigenous leaders compared to a return to colonial land expropriation, we can see how European interest in carbon credits creates incentives for state and private actors to undermine or roll back the hard-won customary rights of frontline indigenous communities in the Amazon.

Key findings

  • Europe’s target of climate neutrality by 2050 and its role in opening up Bolivia to carbon credits.
  • The carbon credit strategy in European policy: a break for polluters.
  • The European Global Gateway strategy and the substantial funds earmarked for Bolivia, which the EU has only disclosed via FOI.
  • The carbon credit agreement that the Multiethnic Indigenous Territory II, known as TIM II, rejects: 88 per cent of the area’s 407,585 hectares is at risk of being controlled by a private foundation for 30 years.
  • In the name of carbon credits, free, prior and informed consent - indigenous of TIM II denounce - has been violated (ILO Convention No. 169).
  • Carbon credits represent a continuation of the colonial approach: a statement by Survival International.
  • From the production of Brazil nuts to carbon credits: a member of the Bolivian national parliament - of Swiss origin and with companies across Europe - proposes legislation on carbon credits whilst simultaneously investing in the sector.
  • Europe in Bolivia: the role of Team Europe (Germany, Sweden, France, Italy and Spain).
  • The false promise that violates the rights of indigenous peoples: a warning from the Solón Foundation.
  • The illusion of change to maintain the status quo: the view of the Green Finance Observatory.
  • Global polluting companies are targeting Bolivia to generate large quantities of carbon credits and continue emitting greenhouse gases: the view of the Bolivian Centre for Legal and Social Studies (CEJIS).

Methodology

The investigation was carried out by four journalists and a photojournalist: two team members in Bolivia and three in Europe. Alongside our fieldwork in the Bolivian Amazon amongst the indigenous communities affected by the carbon credit deal, we carried out research into documents, first-hand accounts, interviews, data analysis, formal requests for data via FOIA, financial investigations, the examination of reports and the analysis of company databases. We divided the areas of investigation amongst the team members, making the most of our multilingual skills and our presence in different countries, and benefited from the support of our mentor, Lionell Faull, for fact-checking, corporate research and information management.

Themes

  • Environment
  • Energy

Publication

ONLINE

  • ‘Carbon fever’ threatens hard-won Indigenous rights in Bolivian Amazon, The Guardian, 15/09/2026

COUNTRIES

  • Belgium
  • Bolivia

Team members

Ruairí Casey

Ruairí Casey is a Berlin-based journalist who specialises in housing, migration and politics

Abby Young-Powell

Abby Young-Powell is an independent British journalist based in Berlin.

Sara Aliaga Ticona

Sara Aliaga Ticona is an Aymara, journalist, visual artist, photojournalist, and filmmaker from Bolivia.

Lisa Mirella Corti

Lisa Mirella Corti is an investigative multimedia journalist.

Maria Cristina Fraddosio

Maria Cristina Fraddosio is an Italian multimedia investigative journalist.

Mentors

Lionel Faull

Lionel Faull is Investigations Editor for Lighthouse Reports, based in Autralia.

Related projects

  • © Michael Bird

    Europe, the Uranium Hell

    BUCHAREST - The EU's focus on achieving energy independence is endangering the environment and the health of its citizens due to the continued exploitation of European uranium resources.

    Meer lezen
  • © rr

    For sale: Hot air

    BUDAPEST - One year ago, the Belgian government purchased two million tonnes of CO₂ emission rights from Hungary. This €26 million investment is intended to help the country meet its obligations under the Kyoto Protocol to reduce emissions by 7.5 per cent by 2012 compared to 1990 levels.

    Meer lezen
  • © Nick Meynen

    The big carbon fraud

    MUMBAI - With financial support from the Fonds Pascal Decroos, Nick Meynen followed carbon credit money flowing from Belgium to India, where he discovered a desert full of mirages. Part from the fraud and abuse, he also noticed the difference in approach between Flanders and Belgium, the buyers of carbon credits.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
ODORHEIU SECUIESC - Two series of multimedia articles were produced thanks to the project. The initial aim was to grow free subscribers to 2,000+, but by the end of the project this target was exceeded, reaching 3,000. The Instagram account also grew by 10%, as the outlet sought to reach a younger adult audience. Some articles were even translated into Romanian in order to provide better multicultural access for Romanian-speaking audiences. This proved tricky, as the outlet's social media channels are all in Hungarian.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

Project Activities

Two series were published, Faith and Future and Rural Realities, both produced by young journalists. They were distributed not only on social media but also in newsletters, as the aim was to grow a direct connection with audiences.

What is the impact?

The aim was to extend direct reach to the audience in order to provide free and independent information and local stories without relying on algorithms. This approach — trying to build a direct link with the community — is considered one of the keystones of better serving a news desert.

The change being sought was to better serve young audiences in local communities. The Instagram growth directly reflects these efforts, thanks in part to young journalists who tend to better understand the wants and needs of young adults.

Project Links

  • Faith and Future series
  • Rural Realities series

Project Pictures

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
SILESIA - Thanks to the project, the jaw.pl editorial team is publishing significantly more Reels and multimedia content produced without the manual work of video editors and camera operators. The new system allows the newsroom to reach new audiences without additional labour costs. Sourcing topics is now much easier, and the processing capabilities using AI tools are constantly evolving as new models emerge.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links

Project Activities

The project team implemented a system for monitoring interesting sources, which now delivers dozens of journalistic topics every day. Thanks to a prompt pipeline system, the newsroom is able to prepare these topics for publication while reflecting the local character, context, and the individual style of the author managing the process. Furthermore, the team deployed a system for generating Reels from journalistic content, which complements the vertical version of the portal and provides engaging material for its social media channels.

What is the impact?

Thanks to the automated system for producing Reels from journalistic materials, the local media outlet is now able to reach a younger demographic through social media. Previously, the newsroom did not have the resources to produce a higher volume of content for these platforms.

The project has led to a greater diversification of the outlet's content, presenting it in a format that is highly accessible to young people. These short, vertical video summaries serve as effective teasers that successfully drive traffic to the full articles on the website.

Project Links

  • jaw.pl

Themes

  • Innovation
  • Journalism & Media

Publication

WEBSITE

  • jaw.pl

SOCIAL MEDIA

  • Facebook
  • YouTube

COUNTRY

Media

Wydawnictwo

Since 1991, Wydawnictwo GM sp. z o.o. is a Polish publisher of local newspapers.

Related projects

    Wablieft goes digital

    MECHELEN - The Wablieft centre for clear language developed an online news channel with quality news for low-literature adults.

    Meer lezen
  • © Apache.be

    Apache Local

    BORGERHOUT - Apache Local was a local journalism project in which news site Apache explored four themes with the help of local citizens and journalists.

    Meer lezen
  • @ reBaltica

    Regional Voices: Reliable News Before Municipal Elections

    RIGA - The project strengthened access to independent local journalism in three municipalities underserved by independent media — Riga, Daugavpils, and Rēzekne — during the pre-municipal election period. It reached young people, women, and Russian-speaking audiences with reliable political and investigative reporting ahead of the municipal elections. The project also strengthened direct connections between journalists and local communities, particularly in Daugavpils and Rēzekne.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
ELENITE/MAMAIA - Mutilated by political decisions that generate huge profits for certain companies, the Romanian and Bulgarian beaches on the Black Sea have become graveyards for tourists who are left at the mercy of natural phenomena exacerbated by the authorities.

Irresponsible decisions by the authorities in Romania and Bulgaria have led to natural and human disasters on the Black Sea beaches.

A flood of epic proportions swept across the beach at the Elenite resort in Bulgaria in 2025, claiming the lives of four people in a matter of minutes. A tragedy that could have been avoided had regulations regarding the protection of floodplains been adhered to.

But the local authorities allowed several tour operators not only to build hotels in the resort’s floodplain, but also to concrete over and narrow the natural channel through which the water could have drained away without affecting either the beach or people’s lives.

In Romania, a mammoth project to extend beaches along the entire coastline has created lethal hazards in the sea: particularly violent rip currents or, conversely, stagnant waters between breakwaters, with enormous pathogen potential, and beaches as hard as concrete.

The one-billion-euro project was carried through to completion against the advice of scientists.

Key Findings

Bulgaria

  • The tragedy on Elenite beach was caused by a series of administrative decisions over the last half-century.
  • The 1980 cadastral plan, for example, made no distinction between the region’s floodplain and the rest of the land.
  • After the 2000s, local authorities issued planning permission for hotels within the floodplain, and the buildings acted as temporary dams.
  • For practical tourism reasons, the floodplain was drastically narrowed and concreted over, causing floodwater to spill onto the beach.
  • None of these illegalities can even be attributed to anyone: the hotel owners who broke the law are hiding behind offshore companies in Cyprus and the Seychelles.

Romania

  • Right from the feasibility study stage, the beach extension project was flawed: the analyses and recommendations of scientists were ignored.
  • Instead of targeted beach extension solutions where erosion was most severe, the preference was for extension along the entire coastline.
  • The sand used was dredged from the seabed – this sand is coarse and contains a high proportion of shells, which has led to the destruction of the beaches.
  • The beach widening and the construction of new breakwaters have increased the number of rip currents, which are extremely dangerous for swimmers.
  • Several marine flora and fauna habitats have been totally or partially destroyed.

Methodology

The project methodology involved the use of legislative, commercial and geographical databases. As part of the project, Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests were submitted, and interviews and field visits were carried out to gather information.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Разливище: Заличената река в "Елените", която уби четирима, 24Chasa, 31/08/2026
  • EXCLUSIV Extinderea plajelor, un dezastru ecologic de un miliard de euro: curenți mortali, țărm distrus, faună și floră marine periclitate, Defapt, 27/08/2026

Countries

  • Bulgaria
  • Romania

Team members

Cătălin Prisacariu

Cătălin Prisacariu is an investigative journalist based in Bucharest, Romania.

Petru Zoltan

Petru Zoltan is a Romanian investigative journalist with nearly two decades of experience.

Stanimir Vaglenov

Stanimir Vaglenov is a Bulgarian journalist who works for Media Group Bulgaria. 

Related projects

    Who Owns Albania’s Coast?

    RRJOLL - From Rrjoll to Himarë, this investigation exposes how Albania's tourism model is driving the transformation of protected areas into luxury “resorts”, enabled by legal reforms and government decisions that favour private interests over environmental protection.

    Meer lezen
  • © under Creative Commons CC0 1.0 UNIVERSAL licence

    Under The Sun: The Hidden Trails of Solar Waste

    ROME / SOFIA / BUCHAREST – Proper recycling of PV panels can generate large quantities of raw materials crucial for the energy transition. Yet, due to the presence of harmful and toxic substances, solar waste can become extremely dangerous when it ends up in the wrong hands.

    Meer lezen
  • © Cosmin Filisan

    Climate Change and Mismanagement Deplete Water Reserves in Europe

    BARUTH / ORTONA / TÂRGU NEAMȚ - Across Europe, communities are facing a water crisis fueled by decades of poor groundwater management and climate change. This investigation examines the causes and consequences of water scarcity related to groundwater reserves in three of the most affected EU countries: Italy, Germany, and Romania.

  • None of these illegalities can even be attributed to anyone: the hotel owners who broke the law are hiding behind offshore companies in Cyprus and the Seychelles.

Romania

  • Right from the feasibility study stage, the beach extension project was flawed: the analyses and recommendations of scientists were ignored.
  • Instead of targeted beach extension solutions where erosion was most severe, the preference was for extension along the entire coastline.
  • The sand used was dredged from the seabed – this sand is coarse and contains a high proportion of shells, which has led to the destruction of the beaches.
  • The beach widening and the construction of new breakwaters have increased the number of rip currents, which are extremely dangerous for swimmers.
  • Several marine flora and fauna habitats have been totally or partially destroyed.

Methodology

The project methodology involved the use of legislative, commercial and geographical databases. As part of the project, Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests were submitted, and interviews and field visits were carried out to gather information.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
ATYRAU - As the EU deepens its energy partnership with Kazakhstan, this investigation goes to the source of the oil that helps power European markets. Reporting from Atyrau, Kazakhstan's oil capital, it explores the social and environmental costs of decades of oil extraction.

In Atyrau, the air is often barely breathable. Residents and activists describe persistent coughing, burning eyes and growing fears over rising cancer rates. Since the arrival of Western oil companies in the 1990s, the city has been transformed from a quiet fishing town into Kazakhstan's oil capital, where almost every sector of the economy depends on the fossil fuel industry. While no direct causal link has been established between oil and gas pollution and cancer, incidence rates have been rising across Kazakhstan, with Atyrau consistently recording some of the country's highest figures. Through on-the-ground reporting, satellite analysis of oil spills, and independent water and soil sampling at sites that residents and activists have long identified as contaminated, this investigation examines the environmental and social costs of oil extraction, and the price local communities are paying for the energy that ultimately reaches European markets.

Methodology:

This investigation combined satellite imagery analysis, environmental sampling, and access to public records. We analysed data from the Transparent World dataset and Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to identify oil spills in the Caspian Sea associated with operations of the Northern Caspian Operating Company (NCOC) consortium. In collaboration with local activists, we collected soil and water samples in areas adjacent to the city to verify the presence of contamination from petroleum products through independent laboratory analysis. We also submitted Freedom of Information requests to European Union institutions and the Italian authorities to obtain official documents concerning EU–Kazakhstan and Italy–Kazakhstan relations, with a particular focus on cooperation related to the country's energy sector.

Key Findings:

  • Laboratory analysis detected contamination from petroleum products, cadmium, chlorides, and sulphites in soil and water samples collected from two heavily affected areas of Atyrau, known as Kvadrat and Tukhlaya Balka. According to local residents and environmental activists, both sites have long been used for the illegal discharge of untreated wastewater generated by oil and gas activities.
  • Using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, we identified four apparent oil spill events within the NCOC operational area in the Caspian Sea at different times during the past year. In response to our questions, the consortium stated that no oil spills have occurred within its area of operations since the beginning of its activities.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Kazakhstan, dove nasce il petrolio, Prismag, 02/09/2026

More to come

    VICENZA / LOTE PARSHURAM - What happens to a Western chemical plant after it closes down due to causing an environmental disaster? Sometimes it travels to other continents. This investigation reveals how a PFAS factory implicated in an Italian environmental scandal was dismantled and rebuilt in India, where production has resumed.

    Meer lezen

    BUCHAREST - For almost 9 years, Romania has been criticised and monitored by the European Commission for allowing the large-scale destruction of several mountain rivers for the purpose of building micro-hydropower plants, without complying with the Water Framework and Habitats Directives.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
RUŽOMBEROK - As demand for paper packaging grows, pressure on Europe’s forests increases. An investigation into Mondi SCP in Slovakia reveals the source of its wood and raises questions about the transparency of logging practices and the future of protected forests.

The global production of paper packaging is surging, yet the rising demand for wood raises questions about sustainability. The Mondi SCP paper mill in Ružomberok is one of Europe's largest paper packaging producers. It uses around 2.2 million cubic metres of wood each year, but the origin of the raw material and the terms of its procurement are not transparent enough.

The investigation has revealed disadvantageous contracts involving state forests, inadequate oversight of logging operations and cases of wood from old-growth forests being used. Thanks to GPS locators, the team of journalists and activists from Slovakia and Germany have uncovered unsustainable logging in Slovakia's national parks.

Experts are warning that supplies of suitable pulpwood are dwindling, and that recycling cannot offset the impact of rising paper consumption. Unfortunately, the political situation in Slovakia is deteriorating. The Slovak government has recently approved a move that puts four national parks back under the control of the state forestry authority rather than conservationists, which makes unsustainable logging more likely.

Themes

  • Environment
  • Industry

Publication

  • Pappe statt Plastik: Wie die EU-Verpackungswende die Nachfrage nach Holz antreibt, MDR, 30/08/2026

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BRUSSELS - It is everywhere, yet invisible. Hawala, an ancient, trust-based money transfer system, moves vast sums of cash around the world every day, leaving almost no trace. No banks. No paper trail. Just a handshake and a code.

Every year, billions of euros legally cross European borders in transparent transfers for private or professional purposes. But alongside these official channels, a parallel system operates in the shadows. Hawala is illegal in many parts of Europe, yet it continues to thrive as a sprawling, highly structured network linked to organised crime. It is used to launder the proceeds of drug trafficking, terrorism and human smuggling on a global scale.

An investigation into terrorism financing in Belgium led the authorities to one of the largest hawala cases ever uncovered in Europe. The inquiry is being led by federal magistrate Vincent Guerra, who was unequivocal: 'These are not amateurs. This is fully professional and beyond anything we could have imagined.'

Now, a team of European investigative journalists, working through the EBU Investigative Journalism Network (a cross-border collaboration of public broadcasters) is joining forces to map the full scope of the network, trace its links to international money-laundering operations, and reveal how legitimate businesses, sometimes unwittingly, have become part of the chain.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
VALLETTA/LISBON/NICOSIA - In Southern Europe, water scarcity demands public investment and raises groundwater prices, but who profits? A three-country investigation identifies commercial actors with disproportionate water privileges in the EU’s most water-scarce countries: Malta, Cyprus & Portugal.

The EU has set objectives to restore and protect the water cycle by recognising water scarcity as a priority in the European Green Deal. The bloc’s Water Resilience Strategy calls for action to address “structural mismanagement of water due to both legal and illegal over-abstraction”. Yet a cross-border investigation covering Malta, Cyprus and Portugal shows that three of the EU’s most water-stressed countries systematically tolerate over-exploitation by for-profit companies.

Main Findings

  • The investigation has documented cases where authorities are neither registering nor controlling commercial abstractions.
  • EU rules allow countries to apply exemptions from prior authorisation and monitoring requirements if administrations consider that individual abstractions will not affect the overall water status. But the actual effects are not known because they do not appear to be thoroughly measured.
  • The Maltese archipelago suffers from water stress and upgrading public water supply costs millions. But the responsible authority’s data show major gaps: under-reporting and registered boreholes attributed to long-defunct companies.
  • Malta’s largest groundwater user is a group of companies that benefits from government tenders and CAP subsidies. The government’s landscaping contractor comes second.
  • Portugal faces extreme water stress, worsened by climate change, while major users (agriculture, tourism, golf resorts) rely on self-extracted groundwater that is poorly monitored and largely invisible to authorities.
  • Private legal status of groundwater, absence of meters, illegal boreholes and weak data block effective pricing, proportional accountability of heavy users, and funding of water infrastructure, shifting drought costs onto public finances.
  • In Cyprus, just 1.4% of recorded abstraction points account for nearly 68% of the total permitted abstraction volume. Meanwhile, audits found poorly documented licensing decisions, known over-abstraction that did not consistently trigger enforcement, and incomplete collection of environmental and resource charges.
  • An unexpected exception is Nicosia’s bicommunal wastewater system: amid Cyprus’s worst drought since records began in 1901, the divided capital’s treatment plant discharged around 11 million cubic metres of reuse-grade water annually for over a decade, helping replenish groundwater and aquifers. A cross-divide project is now building the infrastructure to recover and reuse part of this water for irrigation.

Methodology

The reporters used FOI requests and registry data to piece together evidence of the largest known beneficiaries of the water economy.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

    ALMERIA – The environmental crisis in southern Spain is hitting hard: even drinking water is becoming scarce. A 40-year free-for-all on the “Garden of Europe”, a thriving agricultural industry, has led Almeria to the brink of catastrophe. 

    Meer lezen

    How Drought-provoked Water Scarcity Creates Tensions Between Portugal and Spain

    VIGO – Spain and Portugal share their main rivers, a fact that has promoted diplomatic efforts for the joint management of common bodies of water. However, as extreme droughts become more frequent and intense in the Iberian Peninsula, local populations and legislators alike are struggling to cope with the effects of water scarcity.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
VYHIV / GYE-SUR-SEINE - This investigation uncovers the hidden journey of charcoal, from unpermitted kilns in Ukraine to supermarket shelves across Europe, and the alleged illegal practices behind a market with weak traceability.

Every time we get ready for the summer barbecue season, we forget to look beyond the flames and examine the charcoal itself, revealing a supply chain that is far less transparent than the product suggests. The investigation does just that. Across five European countries, the team identified procurement links connected to a Ukrainian charcoal producer currently under investigation for alleged illegal production practices.

In the Ukrainian village of Vyhiv, an unpermitted pyrolysis kiln operates on agricultural land where a worker shovels charcoal without gloves or a mask. This charcoal ends up on barbecues in France, Poland, Romania, Belgium, or the Netherlands. In autumn 2025, a search at SRL Carbon Pro in Vyhiv led to the seizure of charcoal pallets labeled "Charbon de Bois", unlabeled pallets, and metallic production tanks. Accusations indicate illegal production on agricultural land, supported by state forestry officials understating wood volumes and covering sales without a license.

Customs data shows this charcoal goes to European clients like Grill Impex Polska, Maras Sommer, Flamaco, Beyond Barbecue, and La Forestière du Nord, which sells it under the French brand "Grill O'Bois". Similar investigations exist in Makariv (unauthorized emissions and FSC labels linked to Belgian supply chains) and Shybene (soil contamination exceeding limits for boron, manganese, and arsenic).

An industry source reveals the core scheme: manipulating the "consumption coefficient" (wood-to-charcoal ratio) or buying documents for unused timber to make illegal wood look legal. According to estimates, in the first eight months of 2025, about 10,000 tonnes of Ukrainian charcoal were sold in Europe, with only 1,500 to 3,000 tonnes coming from legal production.

The result is a dual system: a price-driven global chain hampered by delayed EUDR regulation, operating alongside sustainable European projects, like France's Soler Group, struggling against cheap, unverified imports.

Main Findings

  • Document Laundering in Ukraine: Operators manipulate "consumption coefficients" or buy fake documents for unused timber to make illegal wood appear legal. Out of approximately 10,000 tonnes of Ukrainian charcoal sold in Europe in the first eight months of 2025, only 1,500 to 3,000 tonnes came from legal production.
  • Direct Supply Links to EU Retailers: Customs data connects Ukrainian producers under investigation to European buyers in Poland, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, and France (repackaged under domestic brands like "Grill O'Bois").
  • Pollution & Health Hazards: Unlicensed production causes soil contamination with heavy metals (boron, manganese, arsenic) and uses unequipped workers operating without gloves or masks on agricultural land lacking permits.
  • Economic Strain on Clean Producers: Due to unenforced EUDR rules, legal European producers using clean technology (such as Soler Group) face rising local costs and cannot compete against cheap imports brought through intermediaries.

Methodology

  • On-the-Ground Site Visits: Field reporting at unlicensed pyrolysis production sites in Ukrainian villages (Vyhiv, Makariv, Shybene).
  • Customs & Criminal Records:Analysis of customs export data, police search seizures, and judicial investigation filings.
  • Industry Witnesses & Corporate Feedback: Testimony from an anonymous industry insider detailing laundering schemes, alongside business responses (Maras Sommer detailing €300,000 in losses and Soler Group).
  • Expert & Industry Analysis: Integrating market insights from Earthworm Foundation (Lukas Feiler) regarding certification flaws and EUDR regulatory delays.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Dall’Ucraina all’Europa, il caso della carbonella da barbecue che brucia nell’illegalità, Avvenire, 23/08/2026
  • Carbonella da barbecue: in Italia c’è una produzione “doc”, Avvenire, 23/08/2026

More to come

Team members

Marta Abbà

Marta Abbà is an investigative journalists based in Milan.

Viktoriia Hubareva

Viktoria Hubareva is an environmental journalist from Ukraine.

Elisabetta Zavoli

Elisabetta Zavoli is an Italian photographer specialising in environmental documentaries.

Related projects

  • © Marta Abbà

    Italy's Timber Appetite Fuels Albania's Forests Crisis

    TIRANA/MILANO - The destruction of the Balkans' forests continues, especially in the remote areas of Albania where the law doesn't reach and corruption reigns. It's a deep-rooted and local phenomenon, but it's supported by an international dynamic that involves Europe and, above all, the country's best partner in crime: Italy.

    Meer lezen
  • © ANP/AFP

    Illegal South Sudanese Teak Becomes European Garden Furniture in India

    AMSTERDAM - Illegally logged teak from South Sudan goes to India where it is made into furniture before it could end up in stores in Europe. Indian timber traders illegally source the timber from East Africa and export it as an 'Indian' product after processing.

    Meer lezen
  • © Tim Vernimmen

    Dirt cheap service

    BRUSSELS - Though they are right under our feet, soils do not receive much attention. Yet the many free services they provide for us are truly priceless, and they are under pressure. What can we do to prevent all this, and to repair damaged soils, Tim Vernimmen asked eight soil scientists in four countries. In response, they told him about all the things healthy soils can do for us - our food and water needs, our buildings, our health, and the climate - inspiring an article for the popular science magazine EOS that became a plea to stop ignoring the soil. 

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
MINSK - In this investigation, journalists based in five different European countries investigate ties between the EU and Belarus, with a closer look on how far political, economical and social connections have been impacted by the war in Ukraine.

Belarus is a landlocked country in Eastern Europe, bordered by Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. It covers an area of approximately 200,000 square kilometres and has a population of around nine million. Often referred to as 'Europe's last dictatorship', Belarus is a presidential republic in which executive power is concentrated in the hands of President Alexander Lukashenko, who has held power since 1994.

The country has played a controversial role in the ongoing war in Ukraine by acting as a close ally of Russia. By allowing Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for military operations in Ukraine, it has drawn international condemnation and faced sanctions. This has isolated Belarus politically from much of the West, while also making it more dependent on Moscow economically and militarily. The military conflict has also heavily impacted social and economic ties between the EU and Belarus. While some established networks have evolved, new, less formalised forms of collaboration have emerged. This investigation delves into these discrete links.

Contact the team via belarusproject@protonmail.com

AI-Generated Image created by Marina Dulneva

Themes

  • Armed conflict
  • Politics

Publication

  • Hybride Kriegsführung mit Schmuggel-Zigaretten: Rauchen gegen die EU, Falter, 09/12/2025
  • Malgrado le sanzioni, le aziende europee continuano a commerciare con la Bielorussia, Corriere dell'italianità, 11/12/2025

    BRUSSELS - For years, the Belgian political world rolled out the red carpet for Vladimir Putin and his oligarchs. That truth is now becoming all the more painfully clear.

    The Donbass Paradox

    DONETSK - Russian-backed separatists have plundered the rebel-held regions in Ukraine's industrial heartland, creating an economy characterised by fear, hypocrisy and contradiction. How has business transformed since the rebels took control of Ukraine's east?

    Meer lezen

    Kaliningrad, Invisible Battleground

    KALININGRAD - The case of the Russian province Kaliningrad has been causing a war of nerves between East and West. Reports about re-militarisation and information warfare are reminiscent of a Cold War 2.0. Is Europe turning back to a bipolar logic?

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
RRJOLL - From Rrjoll to Himarë, this investigation exposes how Albania's tourism model is driving the transformation of protected areas into luxury “resorts”, enabled by legal reforms and government decisions that favour private interests over environmental protection.

As Albania experiences one of Europe's fastest tourism booms, the country's coastline has become the focus of an unprecedented wave of luxury developments. Behind the promise of economic development, the issue is creating a growing conflict over environmental protection, public resources and decision-making.

This cross-border investigation examines how tourism megaprojects are destroying protected areas, coastal villages and freshwater resources. It explores the environmental consequences of large-scale developments, the legal and political mechanisms enabling them, and their impact on local communities whose livelihoods depend on these fragile ecosystems.

By following multiple case studies - including protected wetlands, coastal construction projects and communities affected by water shortages - it uncovers patterns that extend beyond individual developments, revealing broader structural challenges in Albania's tourism model. It finds that developments promoted as strategic national investments are increasingly expanding into environmentally sensitive areas, while changes in planning and environmental governance have facilitated construction in places previously subject to stronger protection.

The investigation has identified patterns linking public authorities, private investors and regulatory decisions across several major developments that have a real impact on Albania's ecosystem. Together, these findings raise broader questions about transparency, environmental accountability and the long-term sustainability of Albania's tourism model.

Key Findings

  • Albania’s tourism boom is accelerating large-scale construction projects in environmentally sensitive coastal areas.
  • Protected ecosystems are increasingly under pressure from tourism developments promoted as projects of strategic national importance.
  • This model of "development" brings few benefits to local communities, while concentrating profits among a small number of private developers at the expense of Albania's natural resources and ecosystems.
  • Changes in environmental governance and planning procedures have facilitated development in areas previously subject to stronger protection.
  • Changes to legislation governing protected areas have coincided with an acceleration in approvals for large-scale luxury developments, raising serious concerns about transparency and decision-making processes.
  • The investigation identifies a consistent pattern of direct government intervention through legal reforms, strategic investment decisions and planning approvals that has facilitated an unsustainable tourism model, benefiting powerful private interests while accelerating the degradation of Albania's ecosystems.

Methodology

This investigation combined data-driven research with on-the-ground reporting over several months.
The first stage focused on building a comprehensive database of Albania's coastal tourism developments approved between 2015 and 2026. We analysed planning permissions granted by the National Territorial Council (KKT), changes to environmental and planning legislation, strategic investment decisions, environmental impact assessments, and corporate records to identify the investors, developers, architectural firms and public institutions involved in each project.
By cross-referencing these datasets, we identified recurring patterns between legislative changes, the approval of large-scale tourism developments, and environmental concerns repeatedly raised by scientists, NGOs and independent experts. This database also enabled us to select the most representative case studies for further investigation.
The second stage consisted of two weeks of field reporting across Albania. We visited the selected project sites and conducted interviews with local residents, environmental experts, scientists, lawyers, activists, public officials and other stakeholders to assess the environmental and social impacts documented in our data analysis.
Finally, we integrated the documentary research with the field evidence to identify systemic patterns linking legal reforms, strategic investments, planning decisions and environmental degradation. This combined methodology allowed us to move beyond individual case studies and uncover how Albania's current tourism development model is being shaped through the interaction of public policy, private investment and environmental governance.

All the data collected and analysed throughout the investigation can be found on : whoownsthealbaniancoast.com

Themes

  • Corruption
  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Litoral en venta : la maquinaria que privatiza la costa Albanesa, RevistaLate, 27/07/2026
  • “Dosjet e KKT-së” zbulojnë kush e zotëron bregdetin shqiptar, Citizens, 27/07/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Albania

Marta Moreno Guerrero is a Spanish freelance journalist.

Lorin Kadiu is an Albanian media professional with over a decade of experience in journalism and media leadership.

Alexia Galanakis

Alexia is a Chilean freelance journalist based in Spain.

Pablo Fernández Fernández

Pablo Fernández is a Spanish journalist and documentary filmmaker.

Related projects

  • © Jeanna Franke

    Bosnia’s Wood Barons

    SARAJEVO - Around half of Bosnia-Herzegovina is covered by forests and wood is one of the Balkan country’s most valuable natural resources. But instead of developing the nation, some politicians and private companies enrich themselves with the profits of the ‘green gold’. Forests are cut down for private interests and governments and companies in Western-Europe close their eyes to gain cheap wood. 

    Meer lezen
  • © Council for Development and Reconstruction (CDR)

    Tripoli Wastewater Plant: €120m and Two Decades

    TRIPOLI - The investigation looks into the issues that are preventing the expensive wastewater treatment facility in Lebanon from functioning properly.

    Meer lezen
  • © Costanza Musto

    10 Million Tourists A Year In A Small Country

    TIRANA - Albania is experiencing an unprecedented surge in tourism, with more than 7.5 million tourists last year and more than 10 million expected next year. This rapid growth is putting considerable pressure on the country's natural environment.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
GALICIA / IZMIR - As wildfires intensify across the Mediterranean, communities in Spain and Turkey are developing their own strategies to prevent fires, restore damaged ecosystems and protect rural livelihoods, often filling gaps left by public policies.

Across the Mediterranean, wildfires are becoming more frequent, intense and destructive. While public attention often focuses on emergency response and the immediate impacts of fire, less is known about how communities are working to prevent wildfires and restore affected landscapes in the long term.
This cross-border investigation examines grassroots responses to wildfires in Galicia, Spain, and the İzmir region of Turkey. Through field reporting, interviews and visual documentation, the project explores how local communities, farmers, environmental organisations and land managers are developing innovative and traditional approaches to reduce fire risk, regenerate ecosystems and strengthen resilience to climate change.
The investigation also compares two contrasting governance models. In Galicia, communal land ownership structures known as Comunidades de Montes enable collective forest management and prevention initiatives. In Turkey, where forests are largely under state control, community participation is more limited, creating different challenges and opportunities for local action. By highlighting these experiences, the project aims to contribute to broader discussions on wildfire prevention, ecological restoration and climate adaptation across the Mediterranean region.

Key findings

  • Galicia's Comunidades de Montes play a central role in wildfire prevention through collective land management.
  • Nearly half of Galicia's territory is managed under communal ownership structures that encourage local stewardship.
  • Community-led prevention measures include forest clearing, controlled burning and livestock-based fuel management.
  • Turkey's highly centralised forest governance limits the capacity of local communities to participate in prevention efforts.
  • Local initiatives in Turkey exist but often depend on individual leadership and operate within significant legal constraints.
  • Grassroots knowledge and collective action can complement or compensate for shortcomings in institutional wildfire policies.
  • Prevention and ecological restoration receive considerably less attention and investment than fire suppression in both countries.

Methodology

This investigation combines field reporting, data analysis and visual storytelling. The reporting team conducted fieldwork in Galicia (Spain) and the İzmir region (Turkey), spending ten days in each location. During the research, the team interviewed local organisations, environmental NGOs, scientists, community leaders, farmers and residents directly affected by wildfires. We documented prevention, reforestation and land-management initiatives through photography, video and on-the-ground observation. The investigation also draws on forestry databases, land ownership records, academic research, public documents and geospatial analysis tools. All interviews were transcribed, translated where necessary and fact-checked. A comparative approach was used to identify similarities and differences between the two regions, allowing us to examine how governance structures, land ownership models and community engagement influence wildfire prevention and ecological restoration efforts.

GALICIA / IZMIR - As wildfires intensify across the Mediterranean, communities in Spain and Turkey are developing their own strategies to prevent fires, restore damaged ecosystems and protect rural livelihoods, often filling gaps left by public policies.

Across the Mediterranean, wildfires are becoming more frequent, intense and destructive. While public attention often focuses on emergency response and the immediate impacts of fire, less is known about how communities are working to prevent wildfires and restore affected landscapes in the long term.
This cross-border investigation examines grassroots responses to wildfires in Galicia, Spain, and the İzmir region of Turkey. Through field reporting, interviews and visual documentation, the project explores how local communities, farmers, environmental organisations and land managers are developing innovative and traditional approaches to reduce fire risk, regenerate ecosystems and strengthen resilience to climate change.
The investigation also compares two contrasting governance models. In Galicia, communal land ownership structures known as Comunidades de Montes enable collective forest management and prevention initiatives. In Turkey, where forests are largely under state control, community participation is more limited, creating different challenges and opportunities for local action. By highlighting these experiences, the project aims to contribute to broader discussions on wildfire prevention, ecological restoration and climate adaptation across the Mediterranean region.

  • Galicia's Comunidades de Montes play a central role in wildfire prevention through collective land management.
  • Nearly half of Galicia's territory is managed under communal ownership structures that encourage local stewardship.
  • Community-led prevention measures include forest clearing, controlled burning and livestock-based fuel management.

  • Grassroots knowledge and collective action can complement or compensate for shortcomings in institutional wildfire policies.
  • Prevention and ecological restoration receive considerably less attention and investment than fire suppression in both countries.

Methodology

This investigation combines field reporting, data analysis and visual storytelling. The reporting team conducted fieldwork in Galicia (Spain) and the İzmir region (Turkey), spending ten days in each location. item.description:
MISKOLC – Four years after one of Central Europe's most serious river pollution disasters, a cross-border investigation examines what caused the contamination, whether the river has truly recovered, and what lessons remain unanswered.

In 2022, the Sajó River, which flows from Slovakia into Hungary, became the site of one of Central Europe's most serious environmental disasters. Mine water containing arsenic and other heavy metals entered the river system, threatening ecosystems and raising concerns among communities living along its banks. Although emergency measures were introduced, many questions surrounding responsibility, transparency and the long-term environmental consequences have remained unanswered.
This cross-border investigation by Borsod24 and Parameter.sk revisits the disaster several years later to assess what has changed. Through independent laboratory testing, field reporting, interviews with experts, environmental organisations, public officials and local residents, as well as extensive document analysis, the project examines both the causes of the disaster and the current condition of the river.
Beyond reconstructing the events of 2022, the investigation explores whether institutional responses were sufficient, whether pollution risks continue to exist, and what practical measures could prevent similar environmental disasters in the future. By combining scientific evidence with human stories from both sides of the border, the project aims to strengthen public accountability and improve understanding of cross-border environmental protection.

Key Findings

  • The 2022 Sajó River contamination exposed significant weaknesses in environmental monitoring and institutional preparedness.
  • The disaster affected communities in both Slovakia and Hungary, demonstrating the cross-border nature of environmental risks.
  • Independent laboratory measurements are being used to compare current water quality with previous official data.
  • Local residents continue to raise questions regarding transparency, communication and long-term environmental impacts.
  • Experts highlight the importance of improved monitoring systems and stronger international cooperation to prevent similar incidents.

Methodology

The investigation combines documentary research, field reporting, cross-border collaboration and independent scientific verification. The reporting team analysed official documents, historical reporting, environmental data and public records, while conducting interviews with environmental experts, local residents, civil society organisations and public officials. Independent water samples were collected at multiple locations and analysed by an accredited laboratory. The results are compared with previous official measurements and interpreted with expert assistance. The project also includes on-location video reporting documenting the affected areas and the experiences of local communities.

  • Environment
